rules.title: i before e
rules.text: Write i before e, except after c, when the sound is ee. So we write believe and field, but receive and ceiling. There are exceptions, such as neighbor and weigh, where the sound is ay.

rules.title: doubling the final consonant
rules.text: When a short word ends in one vowel and one consonant, double the last letter before adding -ing or -ed. We write running, swimming and stopped. We do not double when the word ends in two consonants or two vowels.

rules.title: dropping silent e before -ing
rules.text: If a word ends in a silent e, drop the e before adding -ing. We write making, taking and hoping. Keep the e when the ending starts with a consonant, as in safely.

rules.title: plurals with -s and -es
rules.text: Most words make a plural by adding -s, as in cats and dogs. If a word ends in s, x, ch or sh, add -es so we can say it, as in boxes and dishes.

rules.title: changing y to ies or ied
rules.text: When a word ends in a consonant and y, change the y to i before adding -es or -ed. One baby becomes two babies, and try becomes tried. When a vowel comes before the y, just add -s, as in boys.

rules.title: soft c and g
rules.text: The letters c and g usually say their soft sounds, s and j, before e, i or y. We hear this in city, ice, giant and gentle. Before a, o or u they sound hard, as in cat and goat.

rules.title: -ful has one l
rules.text: When we add the ending -ful to a word, it has only one l, even though it means full. We write helpful and careful, not helpfull. When we add -ly after it, we write carefully.

rules.title: ck after a short vowel
rules.text: After a short vowel sound at the end of a word, we often write ck for the k sound, as in duck, sock and clock. After a long vowel or a consonant we use k, as in cake and milk.

rules.text: Add -ly to a word to tell how something is done, as in slowly and quickly. If the word ends in y, change the y to i first, as in happily. If it ends in le, drop the e, as in gently.

passages.title: The Red Kite
passages.text: Mia has a red kite. It is a windy day, so she runs to the hill with her dad. The wind pulls the kite up, up, up into the sky. Mia holds the string with both hands. The kite dips and dances above the trees. A small bird flies close and then goes away. Mia laughs and waves. After a while the wind gets soft, and the kite comes down slowly. Mia is a little sad, but her dad says they can come back next week. They walk home and eat warm soup. Mia tells her mom all about the big red kite.

passages.title: The Garden Snail
passages.text: A snail lives in the garden under a big green leaf. It moves very slowly. It leaves a shiny trail behind it, like a silver line on the ground. When the sun is hot, the snail hides in its shell to stay cool. When it rains, the snail comes out to drink and eat. It likes soft leaves and fresh flowers. Children like to watch the snail go. If you touch it, it pulls its soft body inside the shell. The snail is not fast, but it always gets where it wants to go in the end.

passages.title: Bread at the Bakery
passages.text: Every morning, Mr. Lee gets up before the sun. He goes to his small bakery and mixes flour, water, and salt. He pushes and folds the soft dough with his hands. Then he puts the loaves in a hot oven. Soon the whole street smells sweet and warm. At seven o'clock the first people come in. Some buy a loaf of bread, and some buy a bun. A girl named Pia always asks for a bun with seeds on top. Mr. Lee gives it to her with a smile. By noon, all the bread is gone, and he can rest.
qs: When does Mr. Lee get up?
What does Pia like to buy?

passages.title: How Bees Make Honey
passages.text: Honey bees collect a sugary liquid called nectar from flowers. They carry it back to the hive in a special stomach. There, other worker bees take the nectar and pass it from one to another. Enzymes in their bodies change the nectar into simpler sugars. The bees then spread the liquid in small wax cells and fan it with their wings. This removes water until the mixture becomes thick. When the honey is ready, the bees seal each cell with a lid of wax. Honey is stored this way so the colony has food during winter, when few flowers are in bloom.
qs: What do bees do to remove water from the nectar?

passages.title: The Library Bus
passages.text: In a remote region with few roads, the nearest library was once more than a two-hour drive away. Local volunteers solved this problem by turning an old bus into a mobile library. They removed the seats and built shelves along the walls. Twice a week, the bus visits small villages and parks beside the school. Children climb aboard to borrow picture books, while adults choose novels and guides about farming. The volunteers also help people fill out forms and learn to use computers. Because the bus returns regularly, readers can finish a book and exchange it for a new one. Many families say the visits have changed their evenings.
qs: What did the volunteers turn into a library?
How often does the bus visit the villages?

passages.title: Learning to Read a Map
passages.text: A map is a drawing that shows a place from above. To use one well, you should first look for the legend, which explains the symbols. A small blue line might mean a river, while a black square might mean a school. Next, find the scale. It tells you how far a distance on the paper is in real life. For example, one centimeter might equal one kilometer. Finally, look for the compass rose, which shows north. If you turn the map so north points the right way, left and right will match what you see around you. With practice, finding your way becomes easy.
qs: What does the legend of a map explain?
What does the scale tell you?

passages.title: The Invention of the Printing Press
passages.text: Before printing machines existed, every book had to be copied by hand, a process that could take months. Books were therefore rare and costly, and only wealthy institutions could afford more than a handful. In the fifteenth century, a craftsman in Europe developed a press that used movable metal letters. Workers arranged the letters into lines, covered them with ink, and pressed paper against them. The same letters could be reused for many different pages. As a result, books became cheaper and could be produced in far greater numbers. Ideas spread faster than before, literacy rose gradually, and scholars in distant cities could compare each other's work with ease.
qs: What was special about the new press?
What happened to books after the press appeared?

passages.title: Why Cities Grow Near Rivers
passages.text: Many of the world's largest cities began beside rivers, and the reasons are practical. A river supplies fresh water for drinking, cooking, and farming. Its floods leave behind rich soil, which allows farmers to grow abundant crops. Rivers also served as natural highways, so merchants could carry goods by boat long before roads were paved. Settlements that traded successfully attracted craftsmen and workers, and the population gradually increased. However, living near water carries risks, because severe floods can damage homes and fields. Modern engineers therefore build walls, dams, and drainage channels to protect these communities while preserving the advantages that first drew people to the riverbank.
qs: Why were rivers useful to merchants?
What risk comes from living near a river?

passages.title: Sleep and Memory
passages.text: Scientists have found that sleep plays a vital part in how the brain stores memories. During the day, the brain absorbs a huge amount of information, but much of it is fragile. While a person sleeps, the brain replays recent experiences and strengthens the connections that matter. Unimportant details tend to fade. In one common experiment, students who studied a list of words and then slept recalled more of them the next day than students who stayed awake for the same period. Researchers therefore advise learners not to sacrifice rest before an examination. A good night of sleep can be as helpful as an extra hour of study.
qs: What does the brain do during sleep?
What did the students who slept do better?

passages.title: The Economics of Scarcity
passages.text: Economics begins with a simple observation: resources are limited, while human wants are not. This condition, known as scarcity, forces individuals and societies to make choices. Every choice involves an opportunity cost, which is the value of the best alternative that is given up. A town that uses a vacant lot for a parking garage, for instance, forgoes the park that might have stood there. Markets attempt to coordinate such decisions through prices, which signal how valuable a good is relative to others. When a commodity becomes scarcer, its price typically rises, encouraging consumers to economize and producers to supply more. Critics argue, however, that prices alone cannot capture every social consideration.
qs: The value of the best alternative given up
The cost of making a market
What usually happens to a price when a good becomes scarcer?

passages.title: Coral Reef Ecosystems
passages.text: Coral reefs occupy less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they shelter roughly a quarter of all marine species. The foundation of a reef is a colony of tiny animals called polyps, which secrete limestone skeletons. Within their tissues live microscopic algae that perform photosynthesis and supply the polyps with energy. This symbiotic partnership depends on clear, warm, sunlit water. When temperatures rise unusually, the polyps expel the algae, and the coral turns pale in a process called bleaching. Although bleached coral can recover if conditions improve, prolonged stress often proves fatal. Consequently, marine biologists monitor water temperature closely and study resilient coral varieties that may withstand a warming climate.
qs: What do the algae inside polyps provide?
What happens to coral during bleaching?

passages.title: The Rise of Remote Work
passages.text: Advances in broadband and video conferencing have enabled many professionals to perform their duties from home. Proponents highlight several benefits: employees save commuting time, companies can recruit talent from distant regions, and some organizations reduce expenditure on office space. Nevertheless, the arrangement poses distinctive challenges. Spontaneous conversations that once sparked ideas in corridors become rarer, and newcomers may find it harder to absorb a workplace's unwritten customs. Managers must also learn to evaluate performance by results rather than by visible presence. Many firms have consequently adopted a hybrid model, in which staff attend the office on certain days and work remotely on others.
qs: What is a hybrid model of work?
Some days in the office, some at home
What difficulty do newcomers face in remote work?

passages.title: Epistemic Humility in Science
passages.text: A hallmark of rigorous inquiry is provisionality: conclusions are held with confidence proportional to the evidence, and remain open to revision. Scientists distinguish between a hypothesis, which is a testable conjecture, and a theory, which is a well-corroborated explanatory framework that has withstood sustained scrutiny. Falsifiability, the notion that a claim must be capable of being refuted by observation, serves as a demarcation criterion separating empirical statements from dogma. Peer review and replication act as institutional safeguards against error and bias. Yet these mechanisms are imperfect, and practitioners increasingly acknowledge problems such as selective reporting. Epistemic humility, the disposition to recognize the limits of one's knowledge, therefore constitutes a methodological virtue rather than a weakness.
qs: A claim can be refuted by observation
What is the role of replication and peer review?
They guard against error and bias

passages.title: Urban Heat Islands
passages.text: Metropolitan areas frequently register temperatures several degrees higher than their rural surroundings, a phenomenon termed the urban heat island effect. Its causes are manifold. Asphalt and dark roofing absorb solar radiation and release it slowly after sunset, while the scarcity of vegetation limits evaporative cooling. Dense buildings also obstruct airflow, and waste heat from vehicles and air conditioners compounds the problem. The consequences include elevated energy consumption, degraded air quality, and heightened risk for vulnerable residents during heat waves. Mitigation strategies encompass reflective roofing materials, expanded tree canopy, and green roofs. Planners must weigh the cost of these interventions against their considerable long-term public benefits.
qs: Why does vegetation reduce urban heat?
Which is a mitigation strategy mentioned?

passages.title: Cognitive Biases in Judgment
passages.text: Human reasoning, though remarkably capable, is susceptible to systematic distortions known as cognitive biases. Confirmation bias, for instance, leads people to seek and favor information that corroborates their existing beliefs while discounting contrary evidence. Anchoring occurs when an initial figure disproportionately influences subsequent estimates, even if that figure is arbitrary. The availability heuristic causes individuals to overestimate the likelihood of events that are vivid or easily recalled. These tendencies are not signs of stupidity; they derive from mental shortcuts that are efficient in familiar circumstances. Nevertheless, in domains such as medicine or finance, unexamined biases can produce costly errors, which is why structured checklists and deliberate dissent are widely recommended.
qs: Favoring information that supports existing beliefs
To reduce costly errors from bias
To remove the need for evidence

passages.title: Pharmacokinetics Explained
passages.text: Pharmacokinetics describes the trajectory of a drug through the body, conventionally summarized by four processes: absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion. Bioavailability denotes the fraction of an administered dose that reaches systemic circulation unchanged. Orally ingested compounds often undergo first-pass metabolism in the liver, which can substantially attenuate their concentration before they reach target tissues. The elimination half-life, the interval required for plasma concentration to diminish by half, informs the dosing schedule and the time needed to attain steady state. Clinicians must adjust regimens in patients with impaired renal or hepatic function, since diminished clearance may cause accumulation and toxicity.
qs: The fraction of a dose reaching circulation unchanged
The time a drug stays in the liver
Why adjust doses in patients with impaired kidney or liver function?

passages.title: Jurisprudence and Precedent
passages.text: Common-law systems rely heavily on the doctrine of stare decisis, under which courts are generally bound to follow the holdings of earlier decisions in analogous cases. This principle promotes predictability, because litigants can anticipate how a tribunal will adjudicate their dispute, and it fosters impartiality by constraining arbitrary discretion. Nonetheless, rigid adherence can perpetuate outdated or inequitable rules. Judges therefore possess tools to distinguish a prior case on its facts, thereby confining its scope, and higher courts may overrule precedent when its rationale has eroded. The tension between stability and adaptability remains a perennial subject of scholarly debate, with commentators differing over how readily doctrine should evolve.
qs: What does stare decisis require of courts?
Following earlier decisions in similar cases
How can a judge avoid following a prior case?
By distinguishing it on its facts
By waiting for a new law only

passages.title: Photovoltaic Grid Integration
passages.text: Integrating photovoltaic generation into electrical grids presents intricate engineering challenges. Solar output is intermittent, fluctuating with cloud cover and diminishing entirely at night, whereas demand follows its own pattern. Grid operators must therefore maintain frequency and voltage stability by dispatching complementary resources, such as hydroelectric plants or battery storage. A well-known difficulty is the so-called duck curve, in which midday solar abundance depresses net demand, followed by a steep ramp in the evening as the sun sets. Inverters, which convert direct current to alternating current, increasingly incorporate sophisticated controls that help stabilize the network. Forecasting algorithms further enable operators to anticipate variability and schedule reserves economically.
qs: Convert direct current to alternating current
What problem does the duck curve describe?
A steep evening ramp in net demand
A shortage of sunlight at noon

passages.title: Sam and the Rain
passages.text: Sam woke up and heard a tap, tap, tap on the window. It was rain! Sam put on his yellow boots and his blue coat. He went outside with a big green umbrella. He jumped in a puddle and the water went splash. A small frog sat on a leaf and looked at him. Sam said, "Hello, frog! Do you like the rain?" The frog said nothing, but it hopped into the pond. Sam smiled and went back home to get warm.
qs: What did Sam see on a leaf?

passages.title: The Sleepy Cat
passages.text: Our cat is named Pip. Pip loves to sleep. She sleeps on the sofa in the morning. She sleeps in a box in the afternoon. At night she wakes up and walks around the house. Pip likes to drink milk from a small bowl. She also likes to play with a ball of string. When I come home from school, Pip runs to the door. Then she rubs her head on my leg. I think she is saying hello.
qs: Where does Pip sleep in the afternoon?
When does Pip walk around the house?

passages.title: A Surprise in the Lunch Box
passages.text: Lena opened her lunch box at school. Inside she found a sandwich, a red apple, and a small note. The note said, "Have a happy day! Love, Mom." Lena smiled. She ate the sandwich first. Then she shared half of the apple with her friend Omar. Omar had forgotten his lunch, so he was very hungry. He said thank you three times. After lunch, the two friends played catch on the grass until the bell rang.
qs: Who did Lena share the apple with?

passages.title: The Ant and the Leaf
passages.text: A little ant found a big leaf on the ground. She wanted to take it home, but the leaf was too heavy. She pushed and pushed, but it did not move. A second ant came to help. Then a third ant came, and a fourth. Together they lifted the leaf and walked all the way to the hill. The little ant said, "I could not do it alone, but we did it together." The ants had a nice green roof for their home.
qs: Why could the little ant not move the leaf?
How did the ants move the leaf?

passages.title: Grandpa's Garden
passages.text: Every Saturday I help Grandpa in his garden. He gives me a small shovel and a watering can. First we dig little holes in the soil. Then we put in tiny seeds and cover them up. I pour water on the soil, but only a little. Grandpa says seeds need water and sun to grow. Last month we planted carrots. Now green leaves are coming out of the ground. Soon we will pull up the orange carrots and eat them for dinner.
qs: When does the child help in the garden?
What did they plant last month?
What do seeds need to grow?

passages.title: The Big Kick
passages.text: Today our class played soccer on the field. Ben is the smallest boy on our team, but he runs very fast. In the game, the ball rolled to Ben. He kicked it hard, and it flew past the other team. Our goalie was Nina. She caught the ball two times and shouted, "Got it!" At the end, our team won by one goal. Everyone clapped. Our teacher gave each of us a cup of cold water.
qs: A boy from the other team
What did the teacher give each child?

passages.title: How a Rainbow Forms
passages.text: A rainbow appears when sunlight shines through tiny drops of water in the air. Sunlight looks white, but it is really made of many colors mixed together. When a ray of light enters a raindrop, it bends and splits into separate colors. The light bounces off the back of the drop and bends again as it leaves. Red light bends the least, and violet light bends the most, so the colors line up in order. To see a rainbow, you must stand with the sun behind you and the rain in front of you. That is why rainbows often show up after a shower.
qs: What do you need to make a rainbow?
Where should the sun be when you look for a rainbow?

passages.title: Why Leaves Change Color
passages.text: In summer, tree leaves are green because they hold a substance called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll helps the leaf use sunlight to make food for the tree. In autumn, the days become shorter and cooler. The tree slows down its food making, and the green chlorophyll breaks down. Then other colors, which were hidden all along, can be seen. These include yellow and orange. Some leaves also make new red colors in autumn. Finally the leaves dry out and fall to the ground, and the tree rests through the winter.
qs: Why do other colors show in autumn?
What happens to the tree in winter?

passages.title: The Seed Swap
passages.text: Every spring, the people on Maple Street hold a seed swap. Neighbors bring small envelopes of seeds from their own gardens. Mr. Okafor brings tomato seeds, and Ella's family brings sunflower seeds. Last year, Ella noticed that an older neighbor named Mrs. Lee had come with empty hands. Her garden had been damaged by a storm. Ella quietly filled an envelope with sunflower seeds and gave it to her. Mrs. Lee was so pleased that she invited everyone to see her new garden in the summer. By July, tall yellow flowers were growing there.
qs: When does the seed swap happen?
Why did Mrs. Lee have no seeds?
What did Ella give to Mrs. Lee?

passages.title: How Magnets Work
passages.text: A magnet is a piece of metal that can pull some objects toward it. Every magnet has two ends, called poles. One is the north pole and the other is the south pole. If you bring two different poles close together, they attract, which means they pull toward each other. If you bring two of the same pole together, they repel, which means they push apart. Magnets attract things made of iron, such as paper clips and nails, but they do not attract wood or plastic. The Earth itself acts like a giant magnet, and that is why a compass needle points north.
qs: What are the two ends of a magnet called?
What happens when two same poles meet?
Which object will a magnet attract?

passages.title: How Penguins Stay Warm
passages.text: Penguins live in some of the coldest places on Earth, yet they stay warm. Their bodies are covered with short, tightly packed feathers that keep out the wind and water. Under the skin, they have a thick layer of fat called blubber. This fat works like a warm blanket. Penguins also have a clever way to share heat. In a storm, thousands of them stand close together in a huddle. The birds on the outside slowly move to the middle, and others take their place on the edge. In this way, every penguin gets a turn to be warm.
qs: What keeps wind and water out?

passages.title: The Lantern and the Firefly
passages.text: A small firefly lived near an old garden. At night, she glowed with a soft light. One evening she met a tall lantern that hung on a post. "My light is stronger than yours," said the lantern proudly. "You are tiny and dim." The firefly said nothing and flew away. Later, a strong wind blew out the lantern's flame, and the garden became dark. A lost hedgehog could not find his way home. The firefly flew in front of him and glowed all the way to his burrow. The lantern learned that a small light can still be a great help.
qs: What did the lantern say about its light?
Why did the garden become dark?

passages.title: How a Bicycle Moves
passages.text: When you ride a bicycle, your legs do the work. Your feet push the pedals, and the pedals turn a large gear at the front. A chain connects this gear to a smaller gear on the back wheel. As the chain moves, it spins the back wheel, and the bike goes forward. Many bicycles have several gears. A low gear makes pedaling easier, which helps when you climb a hill. A high gear lets you go faster on flat ground. The brakes squeeze the wheels with rubber pads to slow the bike down. Always wear a helmet to protect your head.
qs: What connects the front gear to the back wheel?
Which gear helps you climb a hill?
How do the brakes slow the bike?

passages.title: Why the Ocean Is Salty
passages.text: Rain is slightly acidic, and as it falls on rocks it slowly wears them down. Small amounts of minerals dissolve in the water and are carried by streams and rivers toward the sea. When the sun heats the ocean surface, pure water evaporates and rises into the air, but the dissolved salts stay behind. Over millions of years this process has made seawater taste far saltier than the rivers that feed it. Salt does not keep building up forever, however. Some of it settles into the sea floor, and some is taken up by living things. Because inflow and removal roughly match, the saltiness of the open ocean stays remarkably steady. Scientists find it useful to measure this saltiness, since it affects how dense the water is and how currents move through the deep sea.
qs: Where does most ocean salt originally come from?
Minerals washed from rocks by water
What happens to salt when seawater evaporates?
It stays behind in the ocean
Why does the ocean not get saltier forever?
Salt is also removed at about the same rate
Rain washes the salt out of the sea

passages.title: The Night Shift Baker
passages.text: Jonas starts work when most of the town is asleep. At two in the morning the bakery is silent except for the hum of the big oven, and the air already smells of yeast. He weighs flour with careful hands, because a small mistake can spoil a whole batch. By four, the first loaves are rising under damp cloths. He hardly notices the cold outside as the windows fog over. Delivery trucks arrive at five, and by six the shelves are full. Jonas likes the quiet more than the crowds, but he admits that his weekends are strange. While his friends are out in the evening, he is often in bed with the curtains drawn. Still, when a customer says the bread is the best in town, he feels the long hours were worth it.
qs: Why does Jonas weigh the flour carefully?
A small mistake can spoil a batch
What does the passage suggest about Jonas's weekends?
His sleep schedule makes them unusual
He works in a different town

passages.title: A Case for Walking to School
passages.text: Many families drive their children to school, and it is easy to see why. Roads can be busy, and mornings are rushed. Yet I believe more students should walk, and the reasons are practical. First, a twenty-minute walk gives the body gentle exercise before a day spent sitting at a desk. Second, studies of attention suggest that students who move in the morning often concentrate better in early lessons. Third, fewer cars near the school gate means cleaner air and safer crossings for everyone. Some people reply that distance makes walking impossible, and that is fair. For those families, a shared bus or a drop-off a few streets away could capture part of the benefit. The point is not that every child must walk, but that we should stop treating the car as the only sensible choice.
qs: What is the writer's main argument?
More students should walk to school
Which reason does the writer give for walking?
It costs nothing to build roads
What does the writer offer to families who live far away?
A shared bus or a nearby drop-off

passages.title: How Maps Show Hills
passages.text: A flat sheet of paper cannot easily show that a land surface rises and falls, so mapmakers developed contour lines. Each line joins points of equal height above sea level. If you walked along one line, you would stay at the same level the whole way. When lines are packed closely together, the ground climbs or drops steeply; when they are spread far apart, the slope is gentle. A set of small circles inside one another usually marks a hilltop, with the smallest circle at the peak. Hikers learn to read these patterns before a trip, since a route that looks short on a map may involve a hard climb. Contour lines also help engineers decide where to build roads and where water is likely to flow after heavy rain.
qs: What does one contour line connect?
What do closely packed lines mean?
Why might a short route on a map be hard?

passages.title: The Lighthouse Keeper's Letter
passages.text: Dear Ana, the storm came in on Tuesday and has not left. From the lamp room I can see waves breaking over the rocks, white against a gray sky. Every evening I climb the one hundred and twelve steps to light the great lamp, then climb down again to wind the clock that turns it. My knees complain, but the work matters. Last night a small fishing boat appeared out of the dark, and I watched its lantern bob until it passed the rocks safely. I wondered who was aboard and whether they knew how much I had been watching. The supply boat cannot reach us until the sea calms, so I am rationing tea. Write soon and tell me about the garden. I miss the green. Your brother, Tomas.
qs: Why does Tomas climb the steps each evening?
The supply boat cannot arrive in the storm
How does Tomas feel about the fishing boat?

passages.title: Why Currencies Hold Value
passages.text: Money has worth largely because people agree that it does. A paper note costs almost nothing to print, yet shopkeepers accept it in exchange for goods, since they expect others to accept it in turn. This shared confidence is fragile. When a government issues far more money than the economy can absorb, each unit buys less, and the resulting rise in prices is called inflation. In extreme cases, trust collapses, and people retreat to barter or to foreign currency. To prevent this, many countries delegate monetary policy to an independent institution that adjusts the supply of money and the cost of borrowing. Such institutions aim for gradual, predictable price growth rather than sudden swings. The underlying lesson is that money is a social arrangement, sustained by expectation as much as by any physical backing.
qs: According to the passage, why does money have value?
It is made of precious metal
What can be inferred about money without trust?

passages.title: The Evolution of Written Language
passages.text: Early writing did not begin as an attempt to record speech. The oldest known marks were tallies, tokens and simple pictures used to keep track of goods. Over time, scribes found that a picture could stand not only for an object but also for its sound, which allowed them to write names and abstract ideas that could not be drawn. This conceptual leap, from representing things to representing sounds, eventually produced alphabets, in which a small set of symbols can be recombined to form any word. Alphabets are economical, yet they are hardly neutral: spelling often preserves pronunciations that speakers abandoned centuries ago. English is a notorious example, retaining silent letters that reflect earlier forms of the language. Writing therefore functions as both a tool and a historical record, quietly storing traces of how people once spoke.
qs: What were the earliest marks mainly used for?
A few symbols can form any word
They are easy to draw as pictures
Why does English have silent letters?

passages.title: Biodiversity and Resilience
passages.text: An ecosystem containing many species tends to withstand disturbance better than one dominated by a few. The reason is partly statistical: if a drought or disease eliminates one plant, others with different tolerances can fill the gap, so the overall function of the habitat persists. Ecologists describe this as functional redundancy. Diversity also supports interdependent relationships, such as those between flowers and the insects that pollinate them. Where these networks are rich, the loss of a single partner is cushioned. By contrast, large farms planting a single crop are efficient in good years but vulnerable, since one pest adapted to that crop can spread unchecked. This does not mean that every species contributes equally, and some, called keystone species, have disproportionate influence. Nevertheless, the broad principle holds that variety acts as a form of insurance for living systems.
qs: Why do diverse ecosystems resist disturbance better?
Other species can fill the gap left by a loss
What is the risk of single-crop farms?
How is variety described in the final sentence?

passages.title: Algorithms and Everyday Choices
passages.text: Much of what we see online is arranged by algorithms, which are step-by-step procedures that rank or filter information. A recommendation system, for instance, studies what you previously chose and predicts what you may like next. The method is convenient, because it narrows an overwhelming range of options. However, it can also produce a subtle narrowing of experience. If a system consistently shows you material resembling what you already enjoy, you may rarely encounter anything unfamiliar, and your tastes can become more rigid without your noticing. Designers sometimes address this by deliberately inserting unexpected items. Users, too, can counteract the effect by seeking out sources that the system would not suggest. The central point is that a tool optimized for convenience is not automatically optimized for curiosity, and the two goals can pull in different directions.
qs: What is an algorithm in this passage?
A step-by-step procedure for ranking or filtering
What risk does the writer describe?
Seeing mostly material similar to what you already like
What can users do about it?
Seek out sources the system would not suggest

passages.title: Sleep Debt and Performance
passages.text: Many adults assume they can postpone sleep and repay it later, as one would a loan. Research on sleep restriction suggests the analogy is only partly valid. When people sleep a few hours too little each night for several days, their reaction times and attention decline steadily, yet they typically rate their own impairment as mild. This gap between actual performance and perceived ability is particularly troubling, since it may lead tired individuals to make risky decisions, such as driving, with undue confidence. A single long night of rest can restore some function, but evidence indicates that complete recovery from a long accumulated deficit takes considerably longer. The prudent conclusion is not that a late night is disastrous, but that chronic shortage compounds quietly, and that we are poor judges of our own fatigue.
qs: What do people tend to think of their own impairment?
Why is the gap in judgment troubling?
Tired people may take risks with confidence
What does the writer conclude about one late night?

passages.title: The Quiet Gallery
passages.text: On weekday mornings the gallery was nearly empty, which was precisely why Lena preferred it. She stood before a large canvas of a gray harbor, a painting she had passed a dozen times without really looking. Today, however, she noticed a single thread of orange along the far horizon, so faint that it seemed accidental. The more she studied it, the more deliberate it appeared. The painter had not simply recorded a scene; she had placed one warm hope against a field of cold. Lena felt an unexpected tightness in her throat. A guard shuffled past, politely pretending not to notice. For several minutes she did not move. When she finally turned away, the harbor seemed no less gray, but she carried the orange line with her, a small, stubborn brightness she could not easily explain.
qs: What did Lena notice for the first time?
A faint orange line on the horizon
What does the orange line seem to suggest?
A touch of hope against the cold
What can be inferred about Lena's feelings?
She was angry at the guard

passages.title: Coastlines and Rising Seas
passages.text: A coastline is not a fixed boundary but a shifting negotiation between land and water. Waves erode cliffs in one place and deposit sand in another, and storms can rearrange a beach within hours. Against this natural variability, a gradual rise in sea level adds a persistent pressure. Even a modest increase allows storm surges to reach farther inland, so flooding that once occurred rarely may become routine. Communities respond in contrasting ways. Some build walls and barriers, which protect property but can transfer erosion to neighboring shores. Others restore marshes and dunes, which absorb wave energy more flexibly, though they require space. A third option, relocating buildings away from the shore, is costly and emotionally difficult. Each strategy involves trade-offs, and the most suitable choice depends on local geography, available funds and how much risk residents are willing to accept.
qs: How does the writer describe a coastline?
As a shifting negotiation of land and water
What is a drawback of sea walls?
They can move erosion to nearby shores
What does the passage suggest about choosing a strategy?

passages.title: Falsifiability and Scientific Claims
passages.text: A hypothesis earns its scientific standing not by being confirmed but by being exposed to refutation. Philosophers who emphasise falsifiability argue that a claim which forbids nothing explains nothing: if every conceivable observation can be reconciled with it, the claim is empty. Consider a theory predicting that a certain metal will melt at a precise temperature. A single careful experiment showing otherwise would count against it, and that vulnerability is precisely what makes the theory informative. Critics respond that real scientific practice is messier. When a prediction fails, researchers may blame faulty instruments or an auxiliary assumption rather than the central idea, and such defensive moves are often reasonable. The challenge, then, is to distinguish a prudent adjustment from an evasive one. A useful heuristic is whether the modification yields new, testable consequences or merely protects the original claim from scrutiny. Scientific progress, on this account, depends on a willingness to risk being wrong, a discipline that sits uneasily with the natural wish to defend cherished ideas.
qs: According to the passage, why is a claim that forbids nothing a problem?
It is too difficult to state
What do critics say about real scientific practice?
It is messier than the falsifiability ideal
It always rejects failed predictions at once
In the passage, 'evasive' describes an adjustment that
avoids scrutiny of the original claim

passages.title: Information Asymmetry in Markets
passages.text: Classical models often assume that buyers and sellers possess equal knowledge, yet many transactions violate this premise. When one party knows more than the other, the market may behave perversely. A seller of used machinery, for instance, understands its defects far better than any prospective purchaser. Buyers, wary of hidden flaws, offer only an average price, which drives owners of high-quality machines to withdraw from the market, leaving mostly inferior goods behind. This process, known as adverse selection, can cause an otherwise viable market to shrink or collapse. A related hazard arises after an agreement is made: a person who is insulated from the consequences of risk may behave more carelessly than before. Remedies include warranties, independent inspection, and reputational mechanisms, all of which transmit credible signals about quality and thereby narrow the gap between what each side knows. Without such devices, trust must be built slowly, and many beneficial exchanges simply never take place.
qs: Why do owners of high-quality machines leave the market?
Buyers offer only an average price
What is the effect of adverse selection described here?
A market may shrink or collapse
In the passage, 'perversely' suggests behaviour that is

passages.title: Phonemes and Their Variants
passages.text: Linguists distinguish between the sounds a speaker actually produces and the abstract categories a listener perceives. A phoneme is the smallest unit of sound that can distinguish one word from another in a given language. In English, the difference between the initial sounds of pin and bin alters meaning, so the two sounds belong to separate phonemes. However, the p in pin is pronounced with a puff of breath, whereas the p in spin is not, and English speakers rarely notice the difference. These two realisations are called allophones: variants of a single phoneme whose distribution is predictable from the surrounding sounds. What counts as a meaningful contrast is therefore language specific. A distinction that is crucial in one language may be wholly imperceptible to speakers of another, which partly explains why adult learners struggle to hear and reproduce unfamiliar sound contrasts, even after extensive exposure. Infants, by contrast, begin life sensitive to nearly every contrast and gradually tune their perception to the sounds of the surrounding community.
qs: What is a phoneme, according to the passage?
The smallest sound unit that can change a word's meaning
Any sound a speaker can make
A written letter of the alphabet
Why do English speakers rarely notice the two kinds of p?
They are variants of one phoneme
They change the meaning of words
What does the passage suggest about adult learners?
They may not hear contrasts their first language ignores
They always pronounce new sounds perfectly
They cannot learn any new words

passages.title: Structure and Ornament in Building
passages.text: Architectural theorists have long debated the relationship between a building's structure and its ornament. One tradition holds that honest design should reveal how loads are carried: columns should look like supports, and beams like spans. Ornament, in this view, is superfluous at best and deceptive at worst, since it may disguise the true means of construction. An opposing tradition maintains that decoration is not a mere afterthought but an essential language through which a building communicates its purpose and its culture. Historical practice complicates both positions. Many celebrated structures employ concealed steel frames behind elaborate stone facades, so that what appears to bear the weight in fact does not. Whether such a practice is a falsehood or a legitimate artistic convention depends on what one expects architecture to express. The disagreement endures because it concerns not engineering alone but the deeper question of what a building owes to its observers.
qs: What does the first tradition say about ornament?
It may disguise how the building is built
It is the most important part of design
What do many celebrated buildings have behind their facades?
The word 'superfluous' in the passage means

passages.title: Trophic Cascades
passages.text: Ecologists have long recognised that the removal or reintroduction of a single predator can reverberate through an entire food web. Such indirect effects are termed trophic cascades. When a top predator declines, populations of its prey, typically herbivores, may expand unchecked. The herbivores then consume vegetation more intensively, altering plant communities and, in turn, the habitat available to other organisms. In some river systems, the recovery of predatory fish has reduced numbers of small grazing species, allowing algae and aquatic plants to flourish and thereby changing water clarity. Not every ecosystem responds so dramatically, however. Where food webs are intricate and species can switch among many food sources, the influence of any one predator is diluted. Researchers therefore caution against generalising from a few celebrated cases, and they stress that carefully designed field experiments, rather than anecdotes, are necessary to establish how strongly a predator shapes its surroundings. Only then can managers predict the consequences of restoring a lost species to its former range.
qs: What happens when a top predator declines?
Why might a predator have less influence in some ecosystems?
Species can switch among many food sources
Plants grow too slowly to matter
What do researchers recommend to establish a predator's effect?

passages.title: Regression to the Mean
passages.text: A common error in reasoning arises from ignoring the statistical phenomenon known as regression to the mean. Suppose a group of students takes a test and the lowest scorers are given extra tutoring. When they are retested, their average improves, and observers may credit the tutoring. Yet part of the improvement would have occurred regardless. Any measurement combines a stable underlying quality with chance fluctuation, and individuals selected for extreme results are likely to have benefited or suffered from unusually favourable or unfavourable luck. On a second occasion, that luck is unlikely to repeat, so their scores drift back toward the group average. The same logic explains why an exceptional season in sport is often followed by a more ordinary one. To judge whether an intervention truly works, investigators compare treated individuals with a similar untreated control group, because only such a comparison separates genuine effects from mere statistical drift.
qs: Why might the retested low scorers improve without tutoring?
Chance effects are unlikely to repeat
How can investigators judge whether an intervention works?
Compare with a similar untreated group
an irregular change up or down

passages.title: The Encyclopedic Ambition
passages.text: In the eighteenth century, European scholars undertook to gather the whole of human knowledge into a single, orderly compendium. The encyclopedic project reflected a conviction that reason, applied systematically, could illuminate every domain from the mechanical trades to moral philosophy. Contributors insisted that craftsmen's practical expertise deserved the same dignity as abstract learning, and they illustrated their volumes with detailed plates showing tools and processes. Such a work was more than a reference book; it was an argument that knowledge ought to be accessible, cross-referenced, and open to critique. Authorities of the period sometimes regarded the enterprise with suspicion, since a catalogue of knowledge implicitly challenged inherited hierarchies of expertise. Later historians have noted a paradox: the very impulse to classify everything revealed how provisional classifications are, because categories that seemed natural to one generation appeared arbitrary to the next. The ambition endures today in collaborative reference projects of a vastly larger scale.
qs: What did contributors believe about craftsmen's expertise?
It deserved the same dignity as abstract learning
It was too simple to record
Why did some authorities view the project with suspicion?
It challenged inherited hierarchies of expertise
What paradox did later historians notice?
Classifying everything showed classifications are provisional
Knowledge could never be written down

passages.title: The Unreliable Narrator
passages.text: Critics apply the term unreliable narrator to a storyteller whose account the reader has reason to distrust. The unreliability may stem from youthful naivete, deliberate mendacity, or a self-serving blindness to the narrator's own faults. What distinguishes this device from a simple lie is the gap it opens between what is told and what is evidently meant, a gap that invites the reader to act as detective. Sometimes the author plants subtle incongruities: a narrator who protests too vehemently, or whose description of events fails to cohere with the reactions of other characters. The effect is often ironic, since the narrator's confident tone sharpens the reader's awareness of how much is being concealed. Some theorists contend that every narrator is partial to some degree, so that unreliability is a matter of degree rather than kind. Nevertheless, the most memorable examples compel readers to reinterpret an entire work upon discovering the deception.
qs: What invites the reader to act as detective?
The gap between what is told and what is meant
Which is one cause of unreliability named in the passage?
Self-serving blindness to one's own faults

passages.title: Mens Rea and Culpability
passages.text: Criminal jurisprudence traditionally requires two elements for liability: a prohibited act, known as the actus reus, and a culpable mental state, the mens rea. The latter concept recognises that blame is not apportioned solely according to outcomes. A person who causes harm through an unforeseeable accident is regarded differently from one who intends it, even though the consequences may be identical. Legal systems commonly distinguish several grades of culpability, ranging from purposeful action through knowledge and recklessness to mere negligence, the last of which involves a failure to exercise the care expected of a reasonable person. Certain regulatory offences dispense with the mental element entirely, imposing strict liability to encourage vigilance in activities that carry public hazards. Such departures are contentious, for critics argue that punishing the blameless corrodes the moral authority of the law. Defenders reply that administrative efficiency and the protection of the public justify the exception in narrowly defined circumstances.
qs: What does mens rea refer to?
What is negligence, as described here?
Failing to take the care a reasonable person would
Causing harm by an unforeseeable accident
Why do critics object to strict liability?
It punishes people who may be blameless
It requires too much proof of intent

passages.title: Iatrogenesis and Clinical Humility
passages.text: Medicine's capacity to heal is shadowed by its capacity to harm unintentionally. Iatrogenic illness, meaning disease or injury caused by medical treatment itself, ranges from adverse drug reactions to hospital-acquired infections and the cascading consequences of unnecessary investigation. A screening test with imperfect specificity, for example, may yield false positives that provoke anxiety, further invasive procedures, and occasionally complications more serious than the condition feared. Clinicians therefore weigh the prospective benefit of an intervention against its attendant risks, an exercise complicated by the fact that benefits accrue to a population while harms fall upon individuals. The ancient injunction to do no harm is thus better understood as a call for judicious restraint than as a promise of safety. Contemporary practice increasingly emphasises shared decision-making, in which patients receive candid information about uncertainty and participate in selecting among imperfect alternatives, a posture that tempers therapeutic zeal with humility. Such candour demands time and skill, yet it respects the autonomy of the person receiving care.
qs: Illness caused by medical treatment itself
Illness that spreads only in hospitals
Why can a screening test with imperfect specificity cause harm?
False positives may lead to needless procedures
It is too cheap to be reliable

passages.title: Semantic Drift and Etymology
passages.text: Etymology, the study of word origins, reveals that meanings seldom remain fixed. Over generations, a term may undergo amelioration, acquiring a more positive sense, or pejoration, sliding toward the disparaging. A word once denoting a household servant may come to signify a person of rank, while another that began as neutral descriptor decays into an insult. Meanings also broaden, as when a term for a specific tool is extended to any comparable implement, or narrow, as when a general word for animal flesh contracts to denote a single kind. Such shifts rarely announce themselves; they proceed through countless small adjustments in usage until the older sense survives only in fossilised phrases. The tempting assumption that a word's original meaning is its true one, the so-called etymological fallacy, therefore misleads. Usage, not ancestry, determines what a word means, and the historian of language must describe such evolution without lamenting it. Dictionaries, accordingly, record how words are used rather than legislating how they ought to be.
qs: A word's meaning becoming more negative
A word's meaning becoming more positive
Assuming a word's original meaning is its true one
What determines what a word means, according to the passage?

passages.title: Priors and Posteriors
passages.text: Bayesian inference formalises the process by which rational agents revise their beliefs in light of evidence. One begins with a prior probability, an initial degree of belief in a hypothesis, then updates it by considering how likely the observed data would be if the hypothesis were true as opposed to false. The resulting posterior probability may differ markedly from the prior, particularly when the evidence is surprising. A classic illustration concerns diagnostic testing for a rare condition: even a highly accurate test will produce mostly false alarms if the condition afflicts only a tiny fraction of the population, because the prior is so low. Critics object that the selection of a prior is inescapably subjective and may colour the conclusions. Proponents counter that all inference rests on assumptions, and that the Bayesian approach at least makes them explicit, while accumulating evidence tends to overwhelm divergent starting points and drive differing observers toward agreement.
qs: An initial degree of belief before new evidence
The final result after all evidence
A measure of a test's cost
Why can an accurate test produce mostly false alarms for a rare condition?
The prior probability is very low
The condition is easy to detect
What do proponents say about the Bayesian approach?

passages.title: Underdetermination of Theory
passages.text: Philosophers of science have observed that evidence rarely dictates a single theoretical interpretation. This thesis, termed underdetermination, holds that for any finite body of observations there exist multiple, mutually incompatible theories that accommodate them equally well. A related insight, associated with the idea of holism, is that hypotheses are never tested in isolation: a prediction follows only from a hypothesis together with a web of auxiliary assumptions about instruments, background conditions, and measurement. When an observation conflicts with expectation, logic alone cannot specify which strand of the web ought to be revised. Scientists consequently invoke extra-empirical criteria, such as simplicity, scope, and coherence with established knowledge, to adjudicate among rivals. Whether these criteria track truth or merely express pragmatic preference is contested. Sceptics infer that theory choice is partly conventional, whereas realists maintain that the long-term success of mature theories would be inexplicable if they did not approximate the structure of the world.
qs: Several incompatible theories can fit the same observations
Why can't logic alone say which assumption to revise?
Predictions depend on a web of assumptions
How do realists defend theory success?
It would be inexplicable if theories were not roughly true
It proves theory choice is conventional

poems.author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
poems.title: The Eagle
lines: He clasps the crag with crooked hands;
Close to the sun in lonely lands,
Ring'd with the azure world, he stands.
The wrinkled sea beneath him crawls;
He watches from his mountain walls,
And like a thunderbolt he falls.

poems.author: Christina Rossetti
poems.title: Who Has Seen the Wind?
lines: Who has seen the wind?
Neither I nor you:
But when the leaves hang trembling,
The wind is passing thro'.
Who has seen the wind?
Neither you nor I:
But when the trees bow down their heads,
The wind is passing by.

poems.author: Lewis Carroll
poems.title: Jabberwocky
lines: 'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves
Did gyre and gimble in the wabe:
All mimsy were the borogoves,
And the mome raths outgrabe.

poems.author: Emily Dickinson
poems.title: I'm Nobody! Who are you?
lines: I'm Nobody! Who are you?
Are you--Nobody--too?
Then there's a pair of us!
Don't tell! they'd advertise--you know!
How dreary--to be--Somebody!
How public--like a Frog--
To tell one's name--the livelong June--
To an admiring Bog!

poems.author: William Blake
poems.title: The Tyger
lines: Tyger Tyger, burning bright,
In the forests of the night;
What immortal hand or eye,
Could frame thy fearful symmetry?

poems.author: Edward Lear
poems.title: There was an Old Man with a beard
lines: There was an Old Man with a beard,
Who said, "It is just as I feared!--
Two Owls and a Hen,
Four Larks and a Wren,
Have all built their nests in my beard!"

poems.title: Bed in Summer
poems.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
lines: In winter I get up at night
And dress by yellow candle-light.
In summer quite the other way,
I have to go to bed by day.
I have to go to bed and see
The birds still hopping on the tree,
Or hear the grown-up people's feet
Still going past me in the street.
And does it not seem hard to you,
When all the sky is clear and blue,
And I should like so much to play,
To have to go to bed by day?

poems.title: Rain
poems.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
lines: The rain is falling all around,
It falls on field and tree,
It rains on the umbrellas here,
And on the ships at sea.

poems.title: Where Go the Boats?
poems.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
lines: Dark brown is the river,
Golden is the sand.
It flows along for ever,
With trees on either hand.
Green leaves a-floating,
Castles of the foam,
Boats of mine a-boating--
Where will all come home?
On goes the river
And out past the mill,
Away down the valley,
Away down the hill.
Away down the river,
A hundred miles or more,
Other little children
Shall bring my boats ashore.

poems.title: The Land of Counterpane
poems.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
lines: When I was sick and lay a-bed,
I had two pillows at my head,
And all my toys beside me lay,
To keep me happy all the day.
And sometimes for an hour or so
I watched my leaden soldiers go,
With different uniforms and drills,
Among the bed-clothes, through the hills;
And sometimes sent my ships in fleets
All up and down among the sheets;
Or brought my trees and houses out,
And planted cities all about.
I was the giant great and still
That sits upon the pillow-hill,
And sees before him, dale and plain,
The pleasant land of counterpane.

poems.title: My Shadow
poems.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
lines: I have a little shadow that goes in and out with me,
And what can be the use of him is more than I can see.
He is very, very like me from the heels up to the head;
And I see him jump before me, when I jump into my bed.
The funniest thing about him is the way he likes to grow--
Not at all like proper children, which is always very slow;
For he sometimes shoots up taller like an india-rubber ball,
And he sometimes goes so little that there's none of him at all.
He hasn't got a notion of how children ought to play,
And can only make a fool of me in every sort of way.
He stays so close behind me, he's a coward you can see;
I'd think shame to stick to nursie as that shadow sticks to me!
One morning, very early, before the sun was up,
I rose and found the shining dew on every buttercup;
But my lazy little shadow, like an arrant sleepy-head,
Had stayed at home behind me and was fast asleep in bed.

poems.title: The Cow
poems.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
lines: The friendly cow all red and white,
I love with all my heart:
She gives me cream with all her might,
To eat with apple-tart.
She wanders lowing here and there,
And yet she cannot stray,
All in the pleasant open air,
The pleasant light of day;
And blown by all the winds that pass
And wet with all the showers,
She walks among the meadow grass
And eats the meadow flowers.

poems.title: The Wind
poems.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
lines: I saw you toss the kites on high
And blow the birds about the sky;
And all around I heard you pass,
Like ladies' skirts across the grass--
O wind, a-blowing all day long,
O wind, that sings so loud a song!
I saw the different things you did,
But always you yourself you hid.
I felt you push, I heard you call,
I could not see yourself at all--
O wind, a-blowing all day long,
O wind, that sings so loud a song!
O you that are so strong and cold,
O blower, are you young or old?
Are you a beast of field and tree,
Or just a stronger child than me?
O wind, a-blowing all day long,
O wind, that sings so loud a song!

poems.title: The Moon
poems.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
lines: The moon has a face like the clock in the hall;
She shines on thieves on the garden wall,
On streets and fields and harbour quays,
And birdies asleep in the forks of the trees.
The squalling cat and the squeaking mouse,
The howling dog by the door of the house,
The bat that lies in bed at noon,
All love to be out by the light of the moon.
But all of the things that belong to the day
Cuddle to sleep to be out of her way;
And flowers and children close their eyes
Till up in the morning the sun shall arise.

poems.title: The Swing
poems.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
lines: How do you like to go up in a swing,
Up in the air so blue?
Oh, I do think it the pleasantest thing
Ever a child can do!
Up in the air and over the wall,
Till I can see so wide,
River and trees and cattle and all
Over the countryside--
Till I look down on the garden green,
Down on the roof so brown--
Up in the air I go flying again,
Up in the air and down!

poems.title: From a Railway Carriage
poems.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
lines: Faster than fairies, faster than witches,
Bridges and houses, hedges and ditches;
And charging along like troops in a battle
All through the meadows the horses and cattle:
All of the sights of the hill and the plain
Fly as thick as driving rain;
And ever again, in the wink of an eye,
Painted stations whistle by.
Here is a child who clambers and scrambles,
All by himself and gathering brambles;
Here is a tramp who stands and gazes;
And here is the green for stringing the daisies!
Here is a cart run away in the road
Lumping along with man and load;
And here is a mill, and there is a river:
Each a glimpse and gone forever!

poems.title: The Lamplighter
poems.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
lines: My tea is nearly ready and the sun has left the sky.
It's time to take the window to see Leerie going by;
For every night at teatime and before you take your seat,
With lantern and with ladder he comes posting up the street.
Now Tom would be a driver and Maria go to sea,
And my papa's a banker and as rich as he can be;
But I, when I am stronger and can choose what I'm to do,
O Leerie, I'll go round at night and light the lamps with you!
For we are very lucky, with a lamp before the door,
And Leerie stops to light it as he lights so many more;
And oh! before you hurry by with ladder and with light;
O Leerie, see a little child and nod to him to-night!

poems.title: Singing
poems.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
lines: Of speckled eggs the birdie sings
And nests among the trees;
The sailor sings of ropes and things
In ships upon the seas.
The children sing in far Japan,
The children sing in Spain;
The organ with the organ man
Is singing in the rain.

poems.title: Happy Thought
poems.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
lines: The world is so full of a number of things,
I'm sure we should all be as happy as kings.

poems.title: Windy Nights
poems.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
lines: Whenever the moon and stars are set,
Whenever the wind is high,
All night long in the dark and wet,
A man goes riding by.
Late in the night when the fires are out,
Why does he gallop and gallop about?
Whenever the trees are crying aloud,
And ships are tossed at sea,
By, on the highway, low and loud,
By at the gallop goes he.
By at the gallop he goes, and then
By he comes back at the gallop again.

poems.title: Infant Joy
poems.author: William Blake
lines: 'I have no name;
I am but two days old.'
What shall I call thee?
'I happy am,
Joy is my name.'
Sweet joy befall thee!
Pretty joy!
Sweet joy, but two days old.
Sweet joy I call thee:
Thou dost smile,
I sing the while;
Sweet joy befall thee!

poems.title: Laughing Song
poems.author: William Blake
lines: When the green woods laugh with the voice of joy,
And the dimpling stream runs laughing by;
When the air does laugh with our merry wit,
And the green hill laughs with the noise of it;
When the meadows laugh with lively green,
And the grasshopper laughs in the merry scene;
When Mary and Susan and Emily
With their sweet round mouths sing 'Ha ha he!'
When the painted birds laugh in the shade,
Where our table with cherries and nuts is spread:
Come live, and be merry, and join with me,
To sing the sweet chorus of 'Ha ha he!'

poems.title: Under the Greenwood Tree
poems.author: William Shakespeare
lines: Under the greenwood tree
Who loves to lie with me,
And tune his merry note
Unto the sweet bird's throat--
Come hither, come hither, come hither!
Here shall we see
No enemy
But winter and rough weather.
Who doth ambition shun
And loves to live i' the sun,
Seeking the food he eats
And pleased with what he gets--
Come hither, come hither, come hither!
Here shall he see
No enemy
But winter and rough weather.

poems.title: Winter
poems.author: William Shakespeare
lines: When icicles hang by the wall
And Dick the shepherd blows his nail,
And Tom bears logs into the hall,
And milk comes frozen home in pail;
When blood is nipt, and ways be foul,
Then nightly sings the staring owl
Tuwhoo!
Tuwhit! Tuwhoo! A merry note!
While greasy Joan doth keel the pot.
When all around the wind doth blow,
And coughing drowns the parson's saw,
And birds sit brooding in the snow,
And Marian's nose looks red and raw:
When roasted crabs hiss in the bowl--
Then nightly sings the staring owl
Tuwhoo!
Tuwhit! Tuwhoo! A merry note!
While greasy Joan doth keel the pot.

poems.title: Good-Morrow
poems.author: Thomas Heywood
lines: Pack, clouds, away, and welcome day,
With night we banish sorrow;
Sweet air blow soft, mount larks aloft
To give my Love good-morrow!
Wings from the wind to please her mind,
Notes from the lark I'll borrow;
Bird, prune thy wing, nightingale sing,
To give my Love good-morrow;
To give my Love good-morrow
Notes from them both I'll borrow.
Wake from thy nest, Robin-redbreast!
Sing, birds, in every furrow;
And from each hill, let music shrill
Give my fair Love good-morrow!
Blackbird and thrush in every bush,
Stare, linnet, and cock-sparrow!
You pretty elves, amongst yourselves
Sing my fair Love good-morrow;
To give my Love good-morrow
Sing birds, in every furrow!

poems.title: The Daffodils
poems.author: William Wordsworth
lines: I wander'd lonely as a cloud
That floats on high o'er vales and hills,
When all at once I saw a crowd,
A host of golden daffodils,
Beside the lake, beneath the trees,
Fluttering and dancing in the breeze.
Continuous as the stars that shine
And twinkle on the milky way,
They stretch'd in never-ending line
Along the margin of a bay:
Ten thousand saw I at a glance
Tossing their heads in sprightly dance.
The waves beside them danced; but they
Out-did the sparkling waves in glee:--
A Poet could not but be gay
In such a jocund company!
I gazed--and gazed--but little thought
What wealth the show to me had brought;
For oft, when on my couch I lie
In vacant or in pensive mood,
They flash upon that inward eye
Which is the bliss of solitude;
And then my heart with pleasure fills,
And dances with the daffodils.

poems.title: My Heart Leaps Up
poems.author: William Wordsworth
lines: My heart leaps up when I behold
A rainbow in the sky:
So was it when my life began,
So is it now I am a man;
So be it when I shall grow old
Or let me die!
The Child is father of the Man:
I could wish my days to be
Bound each to each by natural piety.

fables.title: The Hare and the Tortoise
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: A HARE one day ridiculed the short feet and slow pace of the Tortoise, who replied,
laughing: "Though you be swift as the wind, I will beat you in a race."
The Hare, believing her assertion to be simply impossible, assented to the proposal;
and they agreed that the Fox should choose the course and fix the goal.
On the day appointed for the race the two started together.
The Tortoise never for a moment stopped,
but went on with a slow but steady pace straight to the end of the course.
The Hare, lying down by the wayside, fell fast asleep.
At last waking up, and moving as fast as he could,
he saw the Tortoise had reached the goal,
and was comfortably dozing after her fatigue.
fables.moral: Slow but steady wins the race.

fables.title: The Ants and the Grasshopper
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: THE ANTS were spending a fine winter's day drying grain collected in the summertime.
A Grasshopper, perishing with famine,
passed by and earnestly begged for a little food.
The Ants inquired of him, "Why did you not treasure up food during the summer?"
He replied, "I had not leisure enough.
I passed the days in singing."
They then said in derision: "If you were foolish enough to sing all the summer,
you must dance supperless to bed in the winter."

fables.title: The Dog and the Shadow
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: A DOG, crossing a bridge over a stream with a piece of flesh in his mouth,
saw his own shadow in the water and took it for that of another Dog,
with a piece of meat double his own in size.
He immediately let go of his own,
and fiercely attacked the other Dog to get his larger piece from him.
He thus lost both: that which he grasped at in the water, because it was a shadow;
and his own, because the stream swept it away.

fables.title: The Crow and the Pitcher
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: A CROW perishing with thirst saw a pitcher, and hoping to find water,
flew to it with delight.
When he reached it,
he discovered to his grief that it contained so little water that he could not possibly get at it.
He tried everything he could think of to reach the water,
but all his efforts were in vain.
At last he collected as many stones as he could carry and dropped them one by one with his beak into the pitcher,
until he brought the water within his reach and thus saved his life.
fables.moral: Necessity is the mother of invention.

fables.title: The Fox and the Grapes
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: A FAMISHED FOX saw some clusters of ripe black grapes hanging from a trellised vine.
She resorted to all her tricks to get at them, but wearied herself in vain,
for she could not reach them.
At last she turned away, hiding her disappointment and saying: "The Grapes are sour,
and not ripe as I thought."

fables.title: The Lion And The Mouse
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: A LION was awakened from sleep by a Mouse running over his face.
Rising up angrily, he caught him and was about to kill him,
when the Mouse piteously entreated, saying: "If you would only spare my life,
I would be sure to repay your kindness."
The Lion laughed and let him go.
It happened shortly after this that the Lion was caught by some hunters,
who bound him by strong ropes to the ground.
The Mouse, recognizing his roar, came and gnawed the rope with his teeth,
and set him free, exclaiming:
"You ridiculed the idea of my ever being able to help you,
not expecting to receive from me any repayment of your favour;
now you know that it is possible for even a Mouse to confer benefits on a Lion."

fables.title: The North Wind and the Sun
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: THE NORTH WIND and the Sun disputed as to which was the most powerful,
and agreed that he should be declared the victor who could first strip a wayfaring man of his clothes.
The North Wind first tried his power and blew with all his might,
but the keener his blasts, the closer the Traveler wrapped his cloak around him,
until at last, resigning all hope of victory,
the Wind called upon the Sun to see what he could do.
The Sun suddenly shone out with all his warmth.
The Traveler no sooner felt his genial rays than he took off one garment after another,
and at last, fairly overcome with heat,
undressed and bathed in a stream that lay in his path.

fables.title: The Fox and the Crow
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: A CROW having stolen a bit of meat, perched in a tree and held it in her beak.
A Fox, seeing this, longed to possess the meat himself,
and by a wily stratagem succeeded.
"How handsome is the Crow," he exclaimed,
"in the beauty of her shape and in the fairness of her complexion!
Oh, if her voice were only equal to her beauty,
she would deservedly be considered the Queen of Birds!"
This he said deceitfully; but the Crow,
anxious to refute the reflection cast upon her voice,
set up a loud caw and dropped the flesh.
The Fox quickly picked it up, and thus addressed the Crow: "My good Crow,
your voice is right enough, but your wit is wanting."

fables.title: The Boy and the Filberts
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: A BOY put his hand into a pitcher full of filberts.
He grasped as many as he could possibly hold, but when he tried to pull out his hand,
he was prevented from doing so by the neck of the pitcher.
Unwilling to lose his filberts, and yet unable to withdraw his hand,
he burst into tears and bitterly lamented his disappointment.
A bystander said to him, "Be satisfied with half the quantity,
and you will readily draw out your hand."
fables.moral: Do not attempt too much at once.

fables.title: The Milk-Woman and Her Pail
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: A FARMER'S daughter was carrying her Pail of milk from the field to the farmhouse,
when she fell a-musing.
"The money for which this milk will be sold, will buy at least three hundred eggs.
The eggs, allowing for all mishaps, will produce two hundred and fifty chickens.
The chickens will become ready for the market when poultry will fetch the highest price,
so that by the end of the year I shall have money enough from my share to buy a new gown.
In this dress I will go to the Christmas parties,
where all the young fellows will propose to me,
but I will toss my head and refuse them every one."
At this moment she tossed her head in unison with her thoughts,
when down fell the milk pail to the ground,
and all her imaginary schemes perished in a moment.

fables.title: The Oak and the Reeds
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: A VERY LARGE OAK was uprooted by the wind and thrown across a stream.
It fell among some Reeds, which it thus addressed: "I wonder how you,
who are so light and weak, are not entirely crushed by these strong winds."
They replied, "You fight and contend with the wind,
and consequently you are destroyed;
while we on the contrary bend before the least breath of air,
and therefore remain unbroken, and escape."

fables.title: The Dog in the Manger
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: A DOG lay in a manger,
and by his growling and snapping prevented the oxen from eating the hay which had been placed for them.
"What a selfish Dog!" said one of them to his companions;
"he cannot eat the hay himself, and yet refuses to allow those to eat who can."

fables.title: The Mountain in Labor
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: A MOUNTAIN was once greatly agitated.
Loud groans and noises were heard,
and crowds of people came from all parts to see what was the matter.
While they were assembled in anxious expectation of some terrible calamity,
out came a Mouse.
fables.moral: Don't make much ado about nothing.

fables.title: The Lamp
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: A LAMP, soaked with too much oil and flaring brightly,
boasted that it gave more light than the sun.
Then a sudden puff of wind arose, and the Lamp was immediately extinguished.
Its owner lit it again, and said: "Boast no more,
but henceforth be content to give thy light in silence.
Know that not even the stars need to be relit."

fables.title: The Camel and the Arab
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: AN ARAB Camel-driver, after completing the loading of his Camel,
asked him which he would like best, to go up hill or down.
The poor beast replied, not without a touch of reason: "Why do you ask me?
Is it that the level way through the desert is closed?"

fables.title: The Fox and the Crane
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: A FOX invited a Crane to supper and provided nothing for his entertainment but some soup made of pulse,
which was poured out into a broad flat stone dish.
The soup fell out of the long bill of the Crane at every mouthful,
and his vexation at not being able to eat afforded the Fox much amusement.
The Crane, in his turn, asked the Fox to sup with him,
and set before her a flagon with a long narrow mouth,
so that he could easily insert his neck and enjoy its contents at his leisure.
The Fox, unable even to taste it, met with a fitting requital,
after the fashion of her own hospitality.

fables.title: The Swallow and the Crow
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: THE SWALLOW and the Crow had a contention about their plumage.
The Crow put an end to the dispute by saying,
"Your feathers are all very well in the spring,
but mine protect me against the winter."
fables.moral: Fair weather friends are not worth much.

fables.title: The Traveler and His Dog
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: A TRAVELER about to set out on a journey saw his Dog stand at the door stretching himself.
He asked him sharply: "Why do you stand there gaping?
Everything is ready but you, so come with me instantly."
The Dog, wagging his tail, replied: "O, master!
I am quite ready; it is you for whom I am waiting."
fables.moral: The loiterer often blames delay on his more active friend.

fables.title: The Cock and the Jewel
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: A COCK, scratching for food for himself and his hens,
found a precious stone and exclaimed: "If your owner had found thee, and not I,
he would have taken thee up, and have set thee in thy first estate;
but I have found thee for no purpose.
I would rather have one barleycorn than all the jewels in the world."

fables.title: The Fox and the Leopard
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: THE FOX and the Leopard disputed which was the more beautiful of the two.
The Leopard exhibited one by one the various spots which decorated his skin.
But the Fox, interrupting him, said, "And how much more beautiful than you am I,
who am decorated, not in body, but in mind."

fables.title: The Ant and the Dove
fables.author: Aesop (translated by Taylor, 1867)
lines: AN ANT went to the bank of a river to quench its thirst,
and being carried away by the rush of the stream, was on the point of drowning.
A Dove sitting on a tree overhanging the water plucked a leaf and let it fall into the stream close to her.
The Ant climbed onto it and floated in safety to the bank.
Shortly afterwards a birdcatcher came and stood under the tree,
and laid his lime-twigs for the Dove, which sat in the branches.
The Ant, perceiving his design, stung him in the foot.
In pain the birdcatcher threw down the twigs, and the noise made the Dove take wing.
