x: stops the message from being sent
makes the email private for ever

workeng.q: What is the 'subject line' of an email?
workeng.a: a short title that says what it is about
x: the first sentence of the letter

workeng.q: You use 'Reply all'. Who gets your answer?
workeng.a: everyone on the original email

workeng.q: Which is the most formal way to ask for something?
workeng.a: Would it be possible to send me the file?

workeng.q: Which word means 'to pass information on to someone'?
workeng.a: forward
workeng.n: You can forward an email to a colleague.

workeng.q: A 'deadline' is ...
workeng.a: the last time to finish something

workeng.q: Which word means the list of things to talk about in a meeting?
workeng.a: agenda

workeng.q: Which word means the written record of what was decided at a meeting?
workeng.a: minutes

workeng.q: You did not hear a point. A polite question is ...
workeng.a: Sorry, could you repeat that, please?

workeng.q: The manager says: Let's move on. This means ...
workeng.a: let us talk about the next thing

workeng.q: The manager says: Let's wrap up. This means ...
workeng.a: let us finish the meeting

workeng.q: 'Action points' are ...
workeng.a: things people agree to do after the meeting

workeng.q: 'To be on track' means ...
workeng.a: to be going as planned

workeng.q: 'To postpone' a meeting means ...
workeng.a: to move it to a later time

workeng.q: You are joining a video meeting and the sound is off. Someone says: You're on mute. You should ...
workeng.a: turn on your microphone

workeng.q: A 'colleague' is ...
workeng.a: a person you work with
x: a person who rents you a flat

workeng.q: 'To brainstorm' means ...
workeng.a: to share many ideas quickly

workeng.q: To 'chair' a meeting means ...
workeng.a: to lead it

workeng.q: You are asked: Why do you want this job? A good answer is ...
workeng.a: I like the work and I want to learn more.

workeng.q: You are asked about a weakness. A thoughtful answer is ...
workeng.a: I sometimes take too long on details, so I now plan my time.
x: I have no weaknesses and I am perfect.

workeng.q: 'Experience' means ...
workeng.a: the work or things you have done before

workeng.q: A 'CV' (or resume) is ...
workeng.a: a short document about your education and work
workeng.n: In the US it is called a resume.

workeng.q: A 'reference' is ...
workeng.a: a person who can say good things about your work

workeng.q: At the end, the interviewer asks: Do you have any questions? A good idea is to ...
workeng.a: ask something about the job or team
x: say no and leave at once

workeng.q: 'Full-time' work means ...
workeng.a: you work the usual full number of hours

workeng.q: 'Part-time' work means ...
workeng.a: you work fewer hours than full time
x: you work all day and night

workeng.q: At the end of the interview you say ...
workeng.a: Thank you for your time.

workeng.q: 'Qualifications' are ...
workeng.a: the exams, courses or training you have

workeng.q: You do not know how to answer a difficult question. A good thing to say is ...
workeng.a: That's a good question. May I think for a moment?

workeng.q: 'To apply for a job' means ...
workeng.a: to send your details and ask to be considered
x: to get the job without asking
to give a job to someone

manners.note: In many English-speaking places people say please when they ask and thank you when they receive, even in shops and for small things.
manners.q: You ask a waiter for water. What is the usual polite way?
manners.a: Could I have some water, please?

manners.note: In many places people wait in a line (a queue) and expect others to wait for their turn. Pushing in front can upset people.
manners.q: A queue has formed at a bus stop. What do most people expect?
manners.a: Join the end of the line and wait your turn.
x: Ask someone to give you their place.

manners.note: For work, appointments and meetings, being on time matters. If you will be late, many people expect a short message in advance.
manners.q: You will be ten minutes late for an appointment. What is helpful?
manners.a: Send a message to say you will be late.

manners.note: How are you? is often just a greeting, not a real question about health. A short answer is expected: Fine, thanks. And you?
manners.q: A colleague says: How are you? A good short reply is ...
manners.a: Fine, thanks. And you?
x: I will tell you about my illness for ten minutes.

manners.note: In many workplaces and schools people use first names, even for managers. Titles such as Dr or Professor are used in some places. If unsure, listen to what others call the person.
manners.q: You are not sure how to address a new manager. A good idea is to ...
manners.a: Listen to how others address them.

manners.note: People often talk about the weather, travel, food or weekend plans with people they do not know well. Questions about money, age or weight can feel too personal.
manners.q: At a party, which topic is usually safe for small talk?
manners.a: The weather or weekend plans

manners.note: Many people like some space between them and others when talking. A handshake or a short smile is a common first greeting. Customs differ, so follow the other person's lead.
manners.q: When you first meet a new person at work, what is a common greeting?
manners.a: A smile and a handshake or a hello

manners.note: In many English-speaking places, looking at the person who is speaking shows you are listening. It is not a rule for everyone, and some people prefer less.
manners.q: In many places, looking at the person who is speaking usually shows ...
manners.a: that you are listening

manners.note: Sorry is used a lot, even for small things like bumping into someone or asking for help. It can mean excuse me and not that you did something wrong.
manners.q: You bump into someone lightly in a shop. What do most people say?
manners.a: Sorry!

manners.note: People often soften a refusal: Thank you, but I can't. Sorry, I'm busy then. A plain No can sound rude to some listeners.
manners.q: Someone invites you to dinner but you cannot go. A polite reply is ...
manners.a: Thank you for asking, but I can't make it.

manners.note: If you are invited to someone's home, many people bring a small gift such as flowers, sweets or a drink. Ask in advance if there is food you cannot eat.
manners.q: You are invited to a friend's home for dinner. What is a common thing to bring?
manners.a: A small gift, such as flowers or sweets
x: Your own meal and your own plate

manners.note: Calling someone very late at night or very early in the morning can be unwelcome, unless it is an emergency. A short message first is often polite.
manners.q: It is 11 at night. You need to ask a friend a small question. What is usually kind?
manners.a: Send a message and wait until the morning.

manners.note: Many people wait until everyone has been served before eating, or until the host starts. Chewing with your mouth closed and saying thank you for the meal are widely appreciated.
manners.q: At a shared dinner, a common polite habit is to ...
manners.a: wait until everyone is served, or the host begins
x: start eating before the food is on the table
leave the table without a word

manners.note: Customs about tips depend on the country and the place. In some countries a tip is expected in restaurants and for some services. In others it is not. If you are not sure, ask or look at the bill.
manners.q: You are in a new country and a restaurant bill is in front of you. A good first step is to ...
manners.a: check the bill and ask what is usual

manners.note: Greetings differ across the English-speaking world. In many business settings a handshake is common. In other settings a wave or hello is enough.
manners.q: You walk into a small office. What is usually enough?
manners.a: A friendly hello

manners.note: Compliments are common, for example on clothes, food or a job well done. A simple Thank you is a good reply.
manners.q: Someone says: I love your jacket! A simple reply is ...
manners.a: Thank you!

manners.note: In many conversations people wait for a pause before speaking. If you must interrupt, say Sorry to interrupt, but ...
manners.q: You want to say something while others are talking. A polite way is ...
manners.a: Sorry to interrupt, but ...

manners.note: In many shared buildings people try to keep noise low in the evening and at night. Neighbours often prefer a polite word to a complaint through others.
manners.q: Your neighbour's music is loud late at night. A calm first step is to ...
manners.a: ask them politely to turn it down
x: shout at them from the window

manners.note: On buses and trains many people let others get off before they get on, and offer seats to older people or those who need them.
manners.q: At a bus door, what do many people do?
manners.a: Let people get off first
x: Wait on the bus for ever

manners.note: Mr and Ms are common titles. Ms does not say whether a woman is married. Many people simply use first names.
manners.q: You are writing to a woman and you do not know if she is married. A safe title is ...
manners.a: Ms

manners.note: Date order differs: 3/4 can mean the third of April or the fourth of March. Writing the month as a word avoids confusion.
manners.q: You write a date for someone in another country. A clear way is ...
manners.a: 3 April 2026

manners.note: What people wear changes with the place and the occasion. For interviews and formal events many people dress neatly. If unsure, ask what is usual.
manners.q: You are unsure what to wear to a work event. A good idea is to ...
manners.a: ask what other people usually wear
x: wear nothing special and never ask

manners.note: A friendly tone helps a lot in English. A request such as Could you ... ? sounds kinder than a command such as Do this.
manners.q: Which request sounds kinder?
manners.a: Could you close the window, please?

rhetlib.d: Starting several phrases or lines in a row with the same words.
rhetlib.ex: Every day I wait, every day I hope, every day I try.

rhetlib.d: Ending several phrases or sentences with the same words.
rhetlib.ex: We worked for the town, we sang for the town, we lived for the town.

rhetlib.d: Three words, phrases or clauses in a row, used for rhythm and force.
rhetlib.ex: The plan was quick, cheap, and clear.

rhetlib.d: Repeating ideas in reverse order, so the pattern runs A-B, then B-A.
rhetlib.ex: People make the town, and then the town makes the people.

rhetlib.d: Putting two opposite ideas side by side in matching form.
rhetlib.ex: Easy to start, hard to finish.

rhetlib.d: Making a point by denying its opposite, like saying 'not bad' to mean good.
Big exaggeration used for effect and not meant literally.
rhetlib.ex: I have told you a million times to shut the gate.

rhetlib.d: Saying something is smaller or milder than it really is, often for humor.
rhetlib.ex: After the flood, he said the house was a little damp.

rhetlib.d: A question asked for effect, not to get an answer.
rhetlib.ex: Who does not like a warm bed on a cold night?

rhetlib.d: Meaning the opposite of what is said, or an outcome opposite to what was expected.
Joining two words of opposite meaning in one phrase.
rhetlib.ex: The room was filled with a deafening silence.

rhetlib.d: Using the same grammar pattern for linked ideas.
rhetlib.ex: She spoke with kindness and acted with courage.

rhetlib.d: Naming a thing by something closely linked to it.
rhetlib.ex: The crown ruled the land for fifty years.

rhetlib.d: Using a part to stand for the whole, or the whole for a part.
Giving human actions or feelings to things that are not human.
rhetlib.ex: The wind whispered secrets to the trees.

rhetlib.d: Speaking to someone absent, a thing, or an idea as if it could hear.
rhetlib.ex: O moon, tell me where my brother sleeps tonight.

rhetlib.d: Using the same word or phrase again and again for emphasis.
rhetlib.ex: Again and again and again the waves came.

rhetlib.d: Starting nearby words with the same sound.
rhetlib.ex: Big brown bears bounced by the bay.

style.q: Which style is this?  "We would be grateful if you could confirm your attendance by Friday."
style.n: Polite stiff phrases like 'we would be grateful' and no contractions signal a formal style.

style.q: Which style is this?  "Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to enquire about the vacancy."
style.n: The set opening and the word 'enquire' are typical of a formal letter.

style.q: Which sentence suits a business letter?
style.a: I am pleased to confirm your appointment on Monday.
x: Yeah, come in Monday, no problem.
Monday is the day the bright sun will greet you.
style.n: A business letter uses full, polite sentences and no slang. The others are too casual or too lyrical.

style.q: Which sentence suits a business letter?
style.a: Please find the invoice enclosed for your records.
x: Here's the bill, thanks a bunch!
Here is a bill that glows like a golden leaf.
style.n: 'Please find ... enclosed' is standard formal letter wording. The others are casual or poetic.

style.q: Which word is more formal: buy, get, or purchase?
style.n: 'Purchase' is the formal word. 'Buy' and 'get' are everyday words.

style.q: Which word is more formal: try, attempt, or have a go?
style.n: 'Attempt' sounds formal. 'Try' is everyday and 'have a go' is casual.

style.q: Which word is more formal: help, assist, or give a hand?
style.n: 'Assist' is the formal choice. 'Give a hand' is casual.

style.q: Which sentence suits a notice from a town council?
style.a: Residents are advised the road will close Tuesday.
x: Heads up, folks, road's shut Tuesday!
On Tuesday the road will sleep beneath grey barriers.
style.n: A council notice is formal: 'residents are advised', no contractions or slang.

style.q: Which style is this?  "The committee has resolved to postpone the meeting until further notice."
style.n: 'Resolved', 'postpone' and 'until further notice' are stiff, official words.

style.q: Which word is more formal: need, want, or require?
style.n: 'Require' is the formal word for something that is needed.

style.q: Which word is more formal: tell, let know, or inform?
style.n: 'Inform' is the formal word. 'Tell' and 'let know' are everyday.

style.q: Which sentence suits a welcome speech at a ceremony?
style.a: Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to this evening's ceremony.
x: Hey everyone, glad you made it!
Welcome, dear hearts, to the evening's gentle glow.
style.n: A formal event opens with a formal greeting. The others are casual or poetic.

style.q: Which style is this?  "Thank you for your prompt reply; I look forward to hearing from you."
style.n: Set phrases like 'look forward to hearing from you' mark a formal letter.

style.q: Which word is more formal: live, stay, or reside?
style.n: 'Reside' is the formal word for living in a place.

style.q: Which style is this?  "Hey, wanna grab pizza after school?"
style.n: 'Hey' and 'wanna' are casual, spoken words.

style.q: Which style is this?  "I'm so tired, I could sleep for a week lol."
style.n: Contractions, 'lol' and a joking boast show a casual style.

style.q: Which sentence suits a message to a friend?
style.a: Thanks a ton for the lift!
x: I wish to express my gratitude for the transport.
Whereas a lift was given, I hereby give thanks.
style.n: Messages to friends are casual: contractions and friendly words. The others are formal or legal.

style.q: Which sentence suits a message to a friend?
style.a: Can't come tonight, sorry! Next time?
x: I regret that I cannot attend this evening.
The night calls, yet I cannot answer.
style.n: A short message with a contraction and a friendly question is casual.

style.q: Which word is more casual: kid, child, or offspring?
style.n: 'Kid' is the casual word. 'Offspring' is formal or scientific.

style.q: Which word is more casual: friend, pal, or associate?
style.n: 'Pal' is a casual word. 'Associate' is a formal word for someone you work with.

style.q: Which word is more casual: father, dad, or parent?
style.n: 'Dad' is the casual, family word.

style.q: Which style is this?  "No worries, I'll sort it out later."
style.n: 'No worries' and the contraction make this relaxed and casual.

style.q: Which style is this?  "That movie was awesome, you gotta see it!"
style.n: 'Awesome' and 'gotta' are casual spoken words.

style.q: Which sentence suits a text to a brother?
x: Dinner has been prepared; kindly attend promptly.
The evening feast awaits upon the table.
style.n: A quick text to a sibling is short and casual, with a contraction.

style.q: Which word is more casual: hello, hi, or greetings?
style.n: 'Hi' is short and casual. 'Greetings' is formal.

style.q: Which style is this?  "Gonna be late, traffic's a nightmare."
style.n: 'Gonna' and dropping words are marks of casual speech.

style.q: Which word is more casual: friend, buddy, or acquaintance?
style.n: 'Buddy' is casual. 'Acquaintance' is a formal word for someone you barely know.

style.q: Which sentence suits a voicemail to a friend?
style.a: Hey, it's me, call me back when you can!
x: Kindly return my call at your earliest convenience.
My voice drifts to you across the silent wires.
style.n: Friends talk casually. The second answer is formal and the third is poetic.

style.q: Which style is this?  "Nah, I'm good, thanks."
style.n: 'Nah' and 'I'm good' are casual replies.

style.q: Which style is this?  "The data suggest a significant correlation between sleep and memory."
style.n: Terms like 'data', 'significant' and 'correlation' are typical of research writing.

style.q: Which style is this?  "This essay argues that trade routes shaped early cities."
style.n: Saying what the essay 'argues' is a common move in academic writing.

style.q: Which style is this?  "Previous studies have examined the effect of sunlight on plant growth."
style.n: Referring to 'previous studies' is a mark of academic writing.

style.q: Which style is this?  "In this paper, we hypothesise that noise reduces reading accuracy."
style.n: 'In this paper' and 'hypothesise' belong to research writing.

style.q: Which sentence suits a science report for a university lab?
style.a: The experiment demonstrates that heat speeds up dissolving.
x: We did a cool test and the sugar went away faster!
The warm water drank the sugar like a thirsty ghost.
style.n: A science report states findings in an objective way. The others are chatty or poetic.

style.q: Which sentence suits a research report?
style.a: The findings show most participants chose the short text.
x: Turns out most people liked the short one better.
The short text sang and the long one slept.
style.n: 'Findings' and 'participants' are research words. The others are casual or poetic.

style.q: Which word is more academic: hypothesis, guess, or hunch?
style.n: A 'hypothesis' is a testable idea in research. 'Guess' and 'hunch' are everyday words.

style.q: Which word is more academic: methodology, way, or trick?
style.n: 'Methodology' is the research word for the methods used in a study.

style.q: Which word is more academic in a research paper: consequently, so, or that's why?
style.n: 'Consequently' fits written research. 'So' is plain and 'that's why' is spoken.

style.q: Which style is this?  "Smith (2019) argues that urban gardens improve community health."
style.n: A name and year in brackets is a citation, a clear sign of academic writing.

style.q: Which style is this?  "Further research is needed to confirm these preliminary results."
style.n: Calling results 'preliminary' and asking for 'further research' is academic style.

style.q: Which style is this?  "The study used a small sample, which limits how far the results can be generalised."
style.n: 'Sample' and 'generalised' are research terms, used to talk about limits of a study.

style.q: Which style is this?  "This chapter reviews three theories of how children learn words."
style.n: Describing what a chapter 'reviews' is typical of academic books.

style.q: Which style is this?  "The authors contend that the model ignores key variables."
style.n: 'Contend' and 'variables' are scholarly words.

style.q: Which sentence suits a school science report?
style.a: The results show that plants in light grew taller.
x: Wow, the plants in light totally grew taller, so cool!
The plants stretched to kiss the golden light.
style.n: A report states results plainly and objectively, without slang or lyrical images.

style.q: Which style is this?  "The tenant shall pay rent on the first day of each month."
style.n: 'The tenant shall' is typical legal wording for a duty in a contract.

style.q: Which style is this?  "This agreement is made between the seller and the buyer."
style.n: Naming the parties of an 'agreement' is how a contract begins.

style.q: Which style is this?  "The party of the first part hereby agrees to the terms set out below."
style.n: 'Party of the first part' and 'hereby' are old legal wording.

style.q: Which style is this?  "Neither party may end this contract without thirty days' written notice."
style.n: Rules about 'parties' and 'notice' are the language of contracts.

style.q: Which sentence suits a contract?
style.a: The supplier shall deliver the goods within ten days.
x: We'll get the stuff to you in about ten days, promise!
The goods will fly to you on the wings of ten days.
style.n: Contracts use 'shall' and exact terms. The others are casual or poetic.

style.q: Which sentence suits a contract?
style.a: The buyer must not resell the goods without written consent.
x: Please don't sell it on, ok? Just ask us first.
Hold these goods close and let none take them.
style.n: Contracts state exact conditions like 'written consent'.

style.q: Which sentence suits a bike rental contract?
style.a: The renter shall return the bike by 5 p.m.
x: Bring the bike back by five, thanks!
Return the bike when the daylight dims.
style.n: 'The renter shall' marks a contract. The others are casual or poetic.

style.q: Which word is more legal: hereby, right now, or today?
style.n: 'Hereby' is a legal word that means 'by this document'.

style.q: Which word is more legal: thereof, of it, or about it?
style.n: 'Thereof' is a legal word that means 'of that'.

style.q: Which word is more legal in a contract: shall, gonna, or might?
style.n: In contracts, 'shall' states a duty. 'Gonna' is casual and 'might' is not firm.

style.q: Which verb is more legal in a contract: terminate, stop, or quit?
style.n: 'Terminate' is the usual contract word for ending an agreement.

style.q: Which style is this?  "All disputes arising under this lease shall be settled by arbitration."
style.n: 'Disputes', 'lease' and 'arbitration' are legal terms.

style.q: Which style is this?  "The undersigned declares that the information given above is true."
style.n: 'The undersigned declares' is a standard legal statement at the end of a form.

style.q: Which style is this?  "The licence is granted to the user and may not be transferred."
style.n: Terms of a licence and 'may not be transferred' are legal wording.

style.q: Which sentence suits a contract about renting a flat?
style.a: The tenant shall keep the flat clean and in good repair.
x: Keep the flat nice and tidy, ok?
The flat is a small bird; keep its nest clean.
style.n: A rental contract states duties with 'the tenant shall'.

style.q: Which style is this?  "The moon spills silver on the sleeping sea."
style.n: Images ('spills silver', 'sleeping sea') are signs of poetry.

style.q: Which style is this?  "Autumn leaves drift down like tired gold coins."
style.n: The simile 'like tired gold coins' is poetic.

style.q: Which style is this?  "Thy gentle voice doth haunt mine ears."
style.n: Old words like 'thy' and 'doth' give a poetic, archaic feel.

style.q: Which style is this?  "Morning wakes the hills in a blush of rose."
style.n: The morning is described as a person who wakes the hills. That is poetic.

style.q: Which style is this?  "O stars, keep watch where weary sailors roam."
style.n: Speaking to the stars with 'O' is a poetic move.

style.q: Which sentence suits a poem?
style.a: The wind hums softly through the sleeping pines.
x: The wind is blowing through the trees tonight.
The wind speed was recorded as twelve knots.
style.n: A poem gives the wind a voice with images. The others state plain facts.

style.q: Which sentence suits a poem?
style.a: Rain taps a lullaby on the window glass.
x: It is raining and the window is wet.
style.n: The rain 'taps a lullaby', an image that suits a poem.

style.q: Which sentence suits a poem about winter?
style.a: Frost lays her lace across the sleeping fields.
x: It froze last night so the fields are white.
Fields shall be considered frozen from December.
style.n: The frost is a person who lays down lace. That is a poetic image.

style.q: Which word is more poetic: slumber, nap, or snooze?
style.n: 'Slumber' is a gentle, old word often found in poems.

style.q: Which word is more poetic: azure, blue, or bluish?
style.n: 'Azure' is a lyrical word for a bright blue, often used in poems.

style.q: Which word is more poetic: morn, morning, or a.m.?
style.n: 'Morn' is a short, old word used in poems for morning.

style.q: Which word is more poetic: ere, before, or earlier?
style.n: 'Ere' is an old poetic word that means 'before'.

style.q: Which word is more poetic: zephyr, wind, or breeze?
style.n: A 'zephyr' is a soft wind, and the word is mostly found in poems.

style.q: Which style is this?  "Her laughter was a river running bright through the quiet hall."
style.n: Her laughter is compared to a river. That image is poetic.

style.q: Which style is this?  "Time, that gentle thief, steals all our summers."
style.n: Time is a thief in this line. Giving time a character is a poetic device.

style.q: Which style is this?  "Please wash your hands before you eat."
style.n: Short, simple words and a clear order make this plain.

style.q: Which style is this?  "Put the cups on the shelf, then wipe the table."
style.n: Short, direct steps with everyday words are plain.

style.q: Which sentence suits a notice for young children?
style.a: Walk, do not run, in the hall.
x: Running in the corridor is prohibited.
Let your feet be soft as whispers.
style.n: Short and easy words are best for young children.

style.q: Which sentence suits a notice for young children at a pool?
style.a: Stay with a grown-up near the water.
x: Minors must be supervised by an adult at all times.
The water sleeps; wake it not alone.
style.n: Easy words and a short sentence are best for young readers.

style.q: Which word is plainer: use, utilise, or employ?
style.n: 'Use' is short and everyday. Plain writing picks the simple word.

style.q: Which word is plainer: show, demonstrate, or exhibit?
style.n: 'Show' is the simple word.

style.q: Which word is plainer: end, terminate, or conclude?
style.n: 'End' is short and everyday.

style.q: Which word is plainer here: buy, purchase, or acquire?
style.n: 'Buy' is the simple word that most people use every day.

style.q: Which style is this?  "Turn left at the shop. The park is on your right."
style.n: Short directions in simple words are plain.

style.q: Which style is this?  "Take one tablet each day with water."
style.n: A short, clear instruction with easy words is plain style.

style.q: Which style is this?  "We close at five. Come back tomorrow."
style.n: Two short sentences with simple words make this plain.

style.q: Which sentence suits plain instructions on a pasta pack?
style.a: Boil the pasta for ten minutes, then drain it.
x: Immerse the pasta in boiling water for ten minutes.
Let the pasta dance in the bubbling pot.
style.n: Pack instructions use short steps and simple verbs.

style.q: Which word is plainer: start, commence, or initiate?
style.n: 'Start' is the plain, everyday word.

pragma.q: Which request is the most polite?
pragma.a: Could you please pass the salt?
pragma.n: 'Could you please' softens a request. A bare order sounds rude.

pragma.q: In a shop, which request is the most polite?
pragma.a: Excuse me, could I have a bag, please?
pragma.n: 'Excuse me', 'could' and 'please' make a request polite.

pragma.q: Which reply is polite when you cannot come to a party?
pragma.a: Thanks for asking, but I can't make it. I hope it goes well!
x: No, I don't want to come.
pragma.n: A polite no thanks the person and says something kind.

pragma.q: Someone gives you a gift. What is the polite thing to say?
pragma.a: Thank you, that is kind of you.
pragma.n: Thanking the giver is polite, even if you already have one.

pragma.q: You bump into someone by mistake. Which is polite?
pragma.a: Sorry, I did not see you.
pragma.n: Saying sorry shows respect.

pragma.q: Which is a polite way to ask a teacher to repeat something?
pragma.a: Sorry, could you say that again, please?
pragma.n: A polite request has 'sorry', 'could' and 'please'.

pragma.q: Which is the polite way to start a phone call to an office?
pragma.a: Hello, may I speak to Ms Lee, please?
pragma.n: On the phone, greet first, then ask with 'may I' and 'please'.

pragma.q: Which is a polite way to interrupt a speaker?
pragma.a: Sorry to interrupt, may I ask a quick question?
x: Stop talking. I have a question.
pragma.n: Apologising and asking permission makes an interruption polite.

pragma.q: You finish dinner and want to leave the table. Which is polite?
pragma.a: May I be excused, please?
pragma.n: Asking permission with 'may I' and 'please' is polite.

pragma.q: Someone says 'Thank you' to you. Which reply is polite?
pragma.a: You're welcome.
pragma.n: 'You're welcome' is the polite reply to thanks.

pragma.q: A shop worker helped you. What is polite to say when you leave?
pragma.a: Thank you for your help. Have a nice day.
pragma.n: Thanking the person is polite.

pragma.q: At work, which is the most polite way to disagree?
pragma.a: I see your point, but I see it a little differently.
pragma.n: A polite disagreement accepts the other view first.

pragma.q: You want to borrow a pencil. Which is polite?
pragma.a: May I borrow your pencil, please?
pragma.n: Asking with 'may I' and 'please' is polite.

pragma.q: Which voicemail is the most polite?
pragma.a: Hi, this is Sam. Please call me back soon. Thank you.
x: Why are you not picking up?
pragma.n: A greeting, 'please' and 'thank you' keep a message polite.

pragma.q: Which is the polite way to ask a stranger for the time?
pragma.a: Excuse me, do you know what time it is?
pragma.n: Start with 'excuse me' and ask in a full sentence.

pragma.q: Which is the most polite way to give a co-worker advice?
pragma.a: Might it help to try a different way?
pragma.n: A question with 'might' offers advice without blaming.

pragma.q: You are full but offered more food. Which reply is the most polite?
pragma.a: No, thank you. It was lovely, but I am full.
pragma.n: Thank the host and give a kind reason.

pragma.q: Which sentence hedges (is less certain)?
pragma.a: It might rain later.
pragma.n: 'Might' shows the speaker is not sure.

pragma.q: Which sentence is less certain?
pragma.a: I think the answer is nine.
x: Nine is the answer, for sure.
pragma.n: 'I think' softens a claim.

pragma.q: Which sentence hedges?
pragma.a: The store is probably closed by now.
pragma.n: 'Probably' shows the speaker is not fully sure.

pragma.q: Which word makes a statement less certain?
pragma.a: maybe
pragma.n: 'Maybe' shows doubt. 'Surely' and 'always' show certainty.

pragma.q: Which sentence is the most cautious?
pragma.a: The results seem to suggest a link.
x: There is a link, full stop.
pragma.n: 'Seem to suggest' is a careful hedge. 'Prove' is certain.

pragma.q: Which sentence hedges?
pragma.a: She may be late.
pragma.n: 'May' means it is possible, not sure.

pragma.q: Which sentence is the least sure?
pragma.a: He could be at home, I guess.
pragma.n: 'Could be' and 'I guess' both show doubt.

pragma.q: Which sentence is hedged?
pragma.a: The data appear to show a small rise.
x: The data show a huge rise.
pragma.n: 'Appear to' keeps the claim careful, and 'small' limits it.

pragma.q: Which phrase softens an opinion?
pragma.a: It seems to me that...
pragma.n: 'It seems to me' marks a view as personal, not a fact.

pragma.q: Which words make a sentence less sure?
pragma.a: sort of
pragma.n: 'Sort of' is a hedge. 'Exactly' and 'totally' are strong.

pragma.q: Which sentence hedges?
pragma.a: That may be too hard for a first try.
x: That is too hard for a first try.
pragma.n: 'May be' gives a careful opinion.

pragma.q: Which claim is the most careful?
pragma.a: Some studies suggest that sleep helps memory.
x: All studies prove sleep helps memory.
pragma.n: 'Some' and 'suggest' limit the claim.

pragma.q: Which sentence hedges?
pragma.a: I am not completely sure, but I believe it is Tuesday.
pragma.n: Saying 'not completely sure' shows doubt.

pragma.q: A doctor wants to be careful. Which sentence is more cautious?
pragma.a: This could be a cold.
pragma.n: 'Could be' leaves room for another cause.

pragma.q: Which sentence is hedged?
pragma.a: It tends to be sunny in July.
x: It is always sunny in July.
It is sunny every July day.
pragma.n: 'Tends to' means usually, not always.

pragma.q: Which phrase shows the speaker is guessing?
pragma.a: I would guess ten people came.
pragma.n: 'I would guess' makes the number a guess.

pragma.q: Which sentence is hedged?
pragma.a: He seems to be happy.
pragma.n: 'Seems to be' shows the speaker is not sure.

pragma.q: Which sentence shows an uncertain plan?
pragma.a: We might go to the park.
x: We are going to the park at two.
pragma.n: 'Might' shows the plan is not fixed.

pragma.q: Which sentence softens bad news?
pragma.a: I am afraid it may not be ready.
pragma.n: 'I am afraid' and 'may' make the news gentler.

pragma.q: Which word is NOT a hedge?
pragma.a: definitely
pragma.n: 'Definitely' shows certainty. The others show doubt.

pragma.q: Someone says "It is a bit cold in here." What do they most likely want?
pragma.a: The window closed
pragma.n: People often hint at a wish by naming a problem. People can mean different things in different places.

pragma.q: A parent says "Your room is a mess." What do they most likely want?
pragma.a: You to tidy it
pragma.n: This is a hint to tidy up. People can mean different things in different places.

pragma.q: Your friend says "I am starving" at lunchtime. What do they most likely mean?
pragma.a: They want to eat soon
pragma.n: 'Starving' here means very hungry. People can mean different things in different places.

pragma.q: A teacher says "Is that your bag in the doorway?" What does she most likely want?
pragma.a: You to move it
pragma.n: The teacher asks a question but wants the bag moved. People can mean different things in different places.

pragma.q: In a meeting, a coworker says "It is already five o'clock." What do they most likely mean?
pragma.a: It is time to finish
pragma.n: At five the work day often ends. People can mean different things in different places.

pragma.q: You share a plan. Your friend says "That is an interesting idea" in a flat voice. What might they mean?
pragma.a: They may not be sure about it
x: They want to do it now
pragma.n: A flat voice may mean doubt, but the person may also be tired or thinking. People can mean different things in different places.

pragma.q: A customer says to the waiter "We have been waiting a long time." What do they most likely want?
pragma.a: Their food soon
pragma.n: The customer hints they want service faster. People can mean different things in different places.

pragma.q: You are still on the tablet at bedtime and Mum says "Look at the time!" What does she mean?
pragma.a: It is time to stop
x: It is time for a trip
pragma.n: Pointing to the time often means 'it is late'. People can mean different things in different places.

pragma.q: A neighbour says "Your music is quite loud tonight." What do they most likely want?
pragma.a: The music turned down
pragma.n: A comment about noise is often a request to be quieter. People can mean different things in different places.

pragma.q: At work someone says "Let us take this offline." What do they most likely mean?
pragma.a: Talk about it later, in private
pragma.n: 'Offline' here means outside the meeting. People can mean different things in different places.

pragma.q: It is pouring with rain and someone says "Nice weather!" What do they most likely mean?
pragma.a: The weather is bad
pragma.n: Saying the opposite is sarcasm, and the tone usually shows it. People can mean different things in different places.

pragma.q: A teacher says "I would like to see everyone's eyes on me." What does she want?
pragma.a: Everyone to look and listen
pragma.n: The teacher asks for attention in an indirect way. People can mean different things in different places.

pragma.q: A colleague writes "Just a reminder that the report is due Friday." What do they most likely want?
pragma.a: The report finished on time
x: The report sent to a friend
pragma.n: A reminder usually means 'please do not forget'. People can mean different things in different places.

pragma.q: You ask a friend to play. They say "I have a lot of homework tonight." What does it probably mean?
pragma.a: They probably cannot play
pragma.n: It is a soft way to say no. People can mean different things in different places.

pragma.q: A shop worker says "We close in five minutes." What do they most likely want?
pragma.a: You to finish shopping
x: You to look for new shoes
You to open the door wide
pragma.n: The worker hints that it is time to finish. People can mean different things in different places.

pragma.q: Someone says "Can you pass the salt?" What are they really asking?
pragma.a: Please pass it
x: Are you able to lift it?
pragma.n: This question is a polite request, not a question about ability.

pragma.q: What does "Would you mind closing the door?" really mean?
pragma.a: Please close it
pragma.n: 'Would you mind' is a polite way to ask.

pragma.q: Which is an indirect way to say "Be quiet"?
pragma.a: Could you keep it down a little?
pragma.n: 'Keep it down' softly asks for less noise.

pragma.q: Which is an indirect way to say "I do not want to go"?
pragma.a: I'm not sure I have the energy tonight.
x: I am so excited to go!
pragma.n: The speaker avoids saying no and hints at a reason.

pragma.q: Which is the most direct request?
pragma.a: Close the door.
x: Would you mind closing the door?
I wonder if the door could be closed.
pragma.n: A direct request is a short command. The others are softer.

pragma.q: Which reply is an indirect no to an invitation?
pragma.a: Oh, I would love to, but I have plans.
pragma.n: Saying 'I would love to, but...' is a gentle way to refuse.

pragma.q: You want a turn on the swing. Which sentence is a hint?
pragma.a: You have been on that swing a long time.
pragma.n: A hint points to the problem and leaves the request unsaid.

pragma.q: Which is an indirect way to end a phone call?
pragma.a: Well, I should let you get on.
pragma.n: The speaker hints that the call should end without saying 'goodbye now'.

pragma.q: Which text is an indirect way to ask a friend to hurry?
pragma.a: Are you nearly ready? Everyone is waiting.
x: Take all the time you need.
pragma.n: The question hints that time is short.

pragma.q: A teacher says "Shall we put our books away now?" What does she mean?
pragma.a: Please put your books away
x: Do you want to talk about books?
pragma.n: 'Shall we' is a soft way to give an instruction.

pragma.q: Which is an indirect way to ask the price?
pragma.a: I wonder how much this costs.
pragma.n: 'I wonder' turns a question into a polite hint.

pragma.q: Which is an indirect way to say "You made a mistake"?
pragma.a: I think there might be a small error here.
pragma.n: 'I think' and 'might' soften the message.

pragma.q: Someone asks "Do you know what time it is?" Which reply is the most helpful?
pragma.a: Yes, it is half past three.
pragma.n: The question is really a request, so give the time.

pragma.q: Which sentence is a hint, not a direct request?
pragma.a: I left my lunch at home.
pragma.n: A hint states a problem and lets the listener offer help.

pragma.q: "I don't suppose you could lend me a pen?" What is this?
pragma.a: A polite, indirect request
pragma.n: 'I don't suppose' makes the request very soft.

pragma.q: Which sentence is an indirect invitation to sit down?
pragma.a: There is a free chair here.
pragma.n: The speaker points to a chair and hints you can sit.

pragma.q: Which is an indirect way to ask someone to move over on a bench?
pragma.a: Is there room for one more?
pragma.n: The question hints you want to sit.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "Every day I wait, every day I hope, every day I try again."
rhetoric.n: The same opening words, every day, begin each part.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "Here the river bends. Here the road ends. Here we rest."
rhetoric.n: Each sentence starts with the same word, Here.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "When the bell rings, we run. When the rain falls, we sing."
rhetoric.n: Both parts open with the same words, When the.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "We will plant the seeds. We will water the soil. We will wait for the sun."
rhetoric.n: Each sentence opens with the same words, We will.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "No fear of the dark, no fear of the storm, no fear of the sea."
rhetoric.n: The opening words No fear of the are repeated.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "The young cheered for the team, the old cheered for the team, and the dog barked for the team."
rhetoric.n: The same closing words, for the team, end each part.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "Rain on the roof was music to me, and wind in the trees was music to me."
rhetoric.n: Both parts end with the same words, was music to me.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "Books were my escape, games were my escape, and the garden was my escape."
rhetoric.n: The same ending words, were my escape, close each part.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "The dog barked, the door opened, the party began."
rhetoric.n: Three short parts in a row build up a rhythm.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "Quick to learn, slow to anger, eager to help."
rhetoric.n: Three similar phrases are listed in a row.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "The plan was simple, cheap, and fast."
rhetoric.n: Three describing words are lined up together.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "Read it, mark it, remember it."
rhetoric.n: Three short commands follow each other.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "Stop, look, and listen before you cross."
rhetoric.n: Three actions are listed in a row.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "Work hard at your play, and play hard at your work."
rhetoric.n: The words work and play swap places in the second half.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "People make the town, and then the town makes the people."
rhetoric.n: The pattern flips: people-town, then town-people.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "Time spends us as we spend our time."
rhetoric.n: Time-spend is reversed to spend-time in the second half.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "She found the song, and the song found her."
rhetoric.n: The order found-song becomes song-found, a reversed pattern.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "Eat to run, do not run to eat."
rhetoric.n: Eat-run is turned around into run-eat.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "Easy to start, hard to finish."
rhetoric.n: Two opposite ideas, easy and hard, sit side by side.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "Young in years, old in wisdom."
rhetoric.n: Young and old are contrasted in matching form.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "Talk is loud, but kindness is quiet."
rhetoric.n: Loud and quiet are placed against each other.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "We were rich in friends and poor in money."
rhetoric.n: Rich and poor are contrasted in matching form.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "The soup was not bad at all."
rhetoric.n: Not bad is a way to say good by denying the opposite.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "He is no fool."
rhetoric.n: No fool means he is clever, said by denying the opposite.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "That is no small gift."
rhetoric.n: No small means large, said by denying the opposite.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "This is no ordinary hill."
rhetoric.n: No ordinary means special, said by denying the opposite.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "I have told you a million times to close the gate."
rhetoric.n: A million times is a big exaggeration.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "This bag weighs a ton."
rhetoric.n: It does not really weigh a ton; the exaggeration stresses how heavy it is.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "I was so hungry I could eat a horse."
rhetoric.n: Nobody could eat a horse; it is an exaggeration for being very hungry.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "The line stretched to the end of the world."
rhetoric.n: A line cannot reach the end of the world; it is a big exaggeration.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "My brother's feet are the size of boats."
rhetoric.n: Feet are not boat-sized; the exaggeration makes a joke.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "After the storm took the roof, he said it was a bit breezy."
rhetoric.n: A huge problem is described as a small one.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "The desert gets a little warm in summer."
rhetoric.n: A scorching desert is called a little warm, making it sound milder.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "She finished the whole marathon and said it was a short jog."
rhetoric.n: A huge effort is made to sound small.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "The flood left us slightly damp."
rhetoric.n: A flood is described as only slightly damp, so the event sounds smaller.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "He lost every game and called it a mild setback."
rhetoric.n: A big loss is called a mild setback.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "Who wouldn't want to be happy?"
rhetoric.n: It is asked for effect; the answer is obvious.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "How many times must I ask you to be quiet?"
rhetoric.n: It is not a real question; it shows annoyance.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "What could be nicer than a warm bed on a cold night?"
rhetoric.n: The question needs no answer; it makes a point.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "Can anyone say that sharing is wrong?"
rhetoric.n: It is asked to make a point, not to get an answer.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "The fire station burned down."
rhetoric.n: A place that fights fires burning is the opposite of what we expect.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "The man who sold locks was robbed because he forgot to lock his own door."
rhetoric.n: The outcome is the opposite of what we would expect.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "Tom stood in the pouring rain and said, What lovely weather for a picnic."
rhetoric.n: Tom says the opposite of what he means.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "The sign saying Please Be Quiet was hung next to a loud bell."
rhetoric.n: The result is the reverse of what a quiet sign should be.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "The room was filled with a deafening silence."
rhetoric.n: Deafening (very loud) and silence (no sound) are opposites joined.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "It was a bittersweet goodbye."
rhetoric.n: Bitter and sweet are opposites joined in one word.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "It is an open secret that the cat sleeps here."
rhetoric.n: Open and secret are opposites joined in one phrase.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "He gave a cruelly kind answer."
rhetoric.n: Cruelly and kind are opposites joined together.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "She spoke with kindness and acted with courage."
rhetoric.n: Both halves share the same grammar pattern.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "By the lake we rested, and by the fire we told stories."
rhetoric.n: Both halves are built in the same grammar pattern.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "To plant is to hope; to water is to care."
rhetoric.n: The two halves follow the same matching grammar.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "The teacher likes to explain, and the students like to ask."
rhetoric.n: Both halves use the same sentence pattern.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "He lost his keys in the snow and his hat in the wind."
rhetoric.n: The two parts share a matching structure.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "The crown ruled the land for fifty years."
rhetoric.n: The crown stands in for the king or queen.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "The press waited outside the door."
rhetoric.n: The press stands in for the news reporters.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "The kettle is boiling, so I will turn it off."
rhetoric.n: The kettle stands in for the water inside it.

rhetoric.q: Which device is this?  "He has read all of Shakespeare."
rhetoric.n: The author's name stands in for his books.

coining.q: The word "biography" has bio (life) and graph (write). What is a biography?
coining.a: a written story of a life
coining.n: Bio means life and graph means write. A biography is the written story of someone's life.

coining.q: The word "astronaut" has astro (star) and naut (sailor). What is the idea?
coining.n: Astro means star and naut means sailor. An astronaut is a sailor among the stars.

coining.q: The word "zoology" has zoo (animal) and logy (study). What is it?
coining.n: Zoo means animal and logy means the study of. Zoology is the study of animals.

coining.q: The word "geology" has geo (earth) and logy (study). What does it study?
coining.n: Geo means earth and logy means the study of. Geology studies rocks and how the earth is made.

coining.q: The word "telegraph" has tele (far) and graph (write). What is the idea?
coining.n: Tele means far and graph means write. A telegraph sent written messages over long distances.

coining.q: The word "bicycle" has bi (two) and cycle (wheel). What does it mean?
coining.n: Bi means two and cycle means wheel or circle. A bicycle has two wheels.

coining.q: The word "octopus" has octo (eight) and pus (foot). What does it mean?
coining.n: Octo means eight and pus means foot. The name means eight-footed, for its eight arms.

coining.q: The word "dinosaur" has deinos (terrible) and sauros (lizard). What does it mean?
coining.n: Deinos means terrible or fearfully great and sauros means lizard. Dinosaur means terrible lizard.

coining.q: What does "tele" mean in telephone, television and telescope?
coining.n: Tele comes from Greek and means far. All three words are about things that are far away.

coining.q: What does "scope" mean in telescope and microscope?
coining.n: Scope comes from a Greek word for look. A scope is a tool for looking.

coining.q: What does "bio" mean in biology and biography?
coining.n: Bio is Greek for life. Biology studies life and a biography tells the story of a life.

coining.q: What does "hydro" mean in hydroelectric power?
coining.n: Hydro is Greek for water. Hydroelectric power makes electricity from moving water.

coining.q: What does "thermo" mean in thermometer?
coining.n: Thermo is Greek for heat. A thermometer measures heat.

coining.q: What does "-ology" mean at the end of biology, zoology and geology?
coining.n: Logy comes from the Greek word for study or word. It names a subject that people study.

coining.q: What does "meter" mean in thermometer and barometer?
coining.n: Meter comes from a Greek word for measure. A meter is a tool or unit for measuring.

coining.q: What does "phone" mean in telephone, microphone and saxophone?
coining.n: Phone is Greek for sound or voice. All three words are about sound.

coining.q: What does "graph" mean in autograph and photograph?
coining.n: Graph is Greek for write or draw. An autograph is self-written and a photograph is drawn with light.

coining.q: What does "micro" mean in microscope and microwave?
coining.n: Micro is Greek for small. A microscope shows small things and a microwave is a very short wave.

coining.q: What does "geo" mean in geography and geology?
coining.n: Geo is Greek for earth. Both words are about the earth.

coining.q: What does "tri" mean in tricycle and triangle?
coining.n: Tri means three. A tricycle has three wheels and a triangle has three angles.

coining.q: Which method made the word "laser"?
coining.n: Laser comes from the first letters of "light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation".

coining.q: The word "radar" comes from the first letters of "radio detection and ranging". What method is this?
coining.n: An acronym is a word made from the first letters of a phrase. Radar is one.

coining.q: Which method made the word "scuba"?
coining.n: Scuba comes from "self contained underwater breathing apparatus", using the first letters.

coining.q: Which method made the word "sonar"?
coining.n: Sonar comes from "sound navigation and ranging", using the first letters.

coining.q: The letters of "ram" stand for random access memory. Which method made this word?
coining.n: An acronym is built from the first letters of a phrase and said as a word.

coining.q: Which method made the word "modem"?
coining.n: Modem squeezes together modulator and demodulator, the two jobs the device does.

coining.q: Which method made the word "pixel"?
coining.n: Pixel blends "pix", short for pictures, with "element": a picture element.

coining.q: The word "bit" came from "binary digit". Which method made it?
coining.n: Bit blends the start of binary with the end of digit.

coining.q: The word "malware" squashes together "malicious" and "software". Which method made it?
coining.n: Malware blends the start of malicious with the end of software.

coining.q: The word "transistor" came from "transfer" and "resistor". Which method made it?
coining.n: Transistor blends the start of transfer with the end of resistor.

coining.q: The word "webinar" squashes web and seminar together. Which method made it?
coining.n: Webinar blends web with seminar: a talk held on the web.

coining.q: The word "emoticon" comes from emotion and icon. Which method made it?
coining.n: Emoticon blends emotion and icon: a small picture that shows a feeling.

coining.q: The word "virus" was an old word used for a new idea in computers: what was the new use?
coining.a: a program that spreads and harms computers
x: a program that cleans a screen
a game played on a computer
coining.n: Virus first named a germ that makes people sick. A computer virus spreads from machine to machine.

coining.q: The animal word "mouse" was used for a new idea in computers: what is it?
coining.a: a small hand tool that moves the pointer
x: a tiny speaker inside a computer
a program that hunts for bugs
coining.n: The tool has a small body and a cord like a tail, so people called it a mouse.

coining.q: In computing, the old word "bug" was used for a new idea. What is it?
coining.n: Bug was an old word for a small fault in a machine. In computing it means a mistake in a program.

coining.q: In computing, the old word "cloud" was used for a new idea. What is it?
coining.a: storage and services on far-away computers
x: a screen that shows the weather
a cooling fan inside a computer
coining.n: Cloud keeps its sky meaning but now names computers far away that store your files.

coining.q: The old word "memory" got a new use in computers: what is it?
coining.a: the place where a computer keeps information
x: a game that tests how well you remember
coining.n: Memory means remembering. A computer's memory holds information for later.

coining.q: The old word "window" got a new use on computers: what is it?
coining.a: a box on a screen that shows a program
x: a gap that lets light into the machine
a button that turns off the screen
coining.n: A window on a screen is a frame you look through to see a program.

coining.q: The old word "web" (a spider net) got a new use: what is it?
coining.a: a network of linked pages on the internet
coining.n: Web was a spider's net of threads. Linked pages look like a net, so the name stuck.

coining.q: The old word "menu" got a new use on screens: what is it?
coining.a: a list of choices to pick from
x: a list of tiny pictures to colour in
coining.n: A menu in a cafe lists dishes to pick. On a screen it lists actions to pick.

coining.q: The old word "folder" got a new use on computers: what is it?
coining.a: a place that holds files together
x: a tool that makes files smaller
a button that hides the screen
coining.n: A paper folder holds papers. A computer folder holds files in the same way.

coining.q: The old word "cell" meant a small room. In science, what new idea did it name?
coining.a: the tiny building block of living things
coining.n: Early scientists saw tiny boxes in plants that looked like small rooms and called them cells.

coining.q: The old word "tablet" meant a flat slab for writing. What is its new use?
x: a flat tool for cutting paper
coining.n: A tablet was a flat surface to write on. Today it names a flat computer you touch.

coining.q: The old word "firewall" stopped fire from spreading in buildings. What is its new use?
coining.a: a program that blocks unwanted network traffic
coining.n: A building firewall stops fire. A computer firewall stops harmful traffic from reaching a computer.

coining.q: Which method made the word "software"?
coining.n: Software joins the whole words soft and ware. It is the soft part you cannot touch.

coining.q: Which two words were joined to make "hardware"?
coining.n: Hardware joins hard and ware. It is the hard parts of a computer that you can touch.

coining.q: Which method made the word "website"?
coining.n: Website joins web and site: a place on the web.

coining.q: Which method made the word "keyboard"?
coining.n: Keyboard joins key and board: a board with keys.

coining.q: Which two words were joined to make "database"?
coining.n: Database joins data and base: a base where data is kept.

coining.q: Which two words were joined to make "download"?
coining.n: Download joins down and load: to load something down onto your device.

coining.q: Which method made the word "upload"?
coining.n: Upload joins up and load: to load something up to another computer.

coining.q: Which two words were joined to make "online"?
coining.n: Online joins on and line: connected on the line to a network.

coining.q: Which method made the word "touchscreen"?
coining.n: Touchscreen joins touch and screen: a screen you touch.

coining.q: Which method made the word "password"?
coining.n: Password joins pass and word: a secret word that lets you pass in.

coining.q: Which method made the word "laptop"?
coining.n: Laptop joins lap and top: a computer for the top of your lap.

regional.q: In the United States people say "elevator". What do people in Britain usually say?
regional.n: In Britain a machine that carries people between floors is usually a "lift". Americans usually say "elevator".

regional.q: In the United States people say "sidewalk". What do people in Britain usually say?
regional.n: In Britain the path beside a road is usually called the "pavement". Americans usually say "sidewalk".

regional.q: In the United States people say "apartment". What do people in Britain usually say?
regional.n: In Britain a home on one floor of a building is usually a "flat". Americans usually say "apartment".

regional.q: In the United States people say "cookie". What do people in Britain usually say?
regional.n: In Britain a small, crisp, sweet baked treat is usually called a "biscuit". Americans usually say "cookie".

regional.q: In the United States people say "candy". What do people in Britain usually say?
regional.n: In Britain, small sugary treats are usually called "sweets". Americans usually say "candy".

regional.q: In the United States people say "gas (for a car)". What do people in Britain usually say?
regional.n: In Britain, fuel for most cars is usually called "petrol". Americans usually say "gas" or "gasoline".

regional.q: In the United States people say "trunk (of a car)". What do people in Britain usually say?
regional.n: In Britain, the storage space at the back of a car is usually called the "boot". Americans usually say "trunk".

regional.q: In the United States people say "hood (of a car)". What do people in Britain usually say?
regional.n: In Britain, the cover over a car engine is usually called the "bonnet". Americans usually say "hood".

regional.q: In the United States people say "diaper". What do people in Britain usually say?
regional.n: In Britain, a baby wears a "nappy". Americans usually say "diaper".

regional.q: Which spelling is usual in Britain for a hue like red or blue?
regional.n: British English usually spells it "colour". The United States usually spells it "color".

regional.q: Which spelling is usual in Britain for the middle point of a circle?
regional.n: British English usually spells it "centre". The United States usually spells it "center".

regional.q: Which spelling is usual in Britain for the shade between black and white?
regional.n: British English usually spells it "grey". The United States usually spells it "gray".

regional.q: Which spelling is usual in Britain for the rubber ring around a wheel?
regional.n: British English usually spells this wheel part "tyre". The United States usually spells it "tire".

regional.q: Which spelling is usual in Britain for protection against attack?
regional.n: British English usually spells it "defence". The United States usually spells it "defense".

regional.q: Which spelling is usual in Britain for a television or radio show?
regional.n: In Britain "programme" is usual for a show or plan. "Program" is used for computer programs in Britain too.

regional.q: Which spelling is usual in Britain for going on a journey (-ing form)?

regional.n: In the United States a big goods vehicle is usually a "truck". People in Britain usually say "lorry".
